nytimes.com.title: Protests in Indonesia Demand Action to Stop Rainforest Fires
nytimes.com.text:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets this week in Indonesia to voice anger at what they see as their government’s failure to stop fires in rainforests that have blanketed their country in a sickening haze.
The demonstrations by students and members of civil society groups began on Monday and spread to more than a half dozen cities across the country including on the island of Borneo, where many of the fires are burning.
These are the latest in a series of protests that have been building since August, in which participants have demanded that the nation’s president, Prabowo Subianto, declare a national emergency and take steps to prevent destructive agricultural practices that many blame for fueling the blazes.
“I have the right to breathe,” read one banner at a rally in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. “Extinguish the fires immediately!”
“The situation has reached a level that is completely, utterly abnormal,” said one protester, Naomi Artika, a law student at the University of Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, a province on Borneo.
Government leaders defended their response, which has not been able to halt the fires.

cnn.com.title: Lions are being poisoned in revenge attacks. Maasai warriors are trying to end the killings
cnn.com.text: After a lifetime spent shadowing wildlife on the plains of Kenya’s Amboseli National Park, Eric Ole Kesoi’s reputation as one of the Maasai’s finest trackers is built on his ability to know where to look. At the end of this search, however, it takes all of his conviction to keep his eyes on the sight before him. At the center of the grisly scene are the gnawed remains of a young cow, peppered with bite wounds made by the pride of lions that lie writhing and panting a few feet away, fighting for their lives. Nine blue-stained tongues loll from foaming mouths, the calling card of an unseen weapon. “Poisoning is really the most brutal form of killing an animal. It’s heart wrenching,” Kesoi tells CNN. “You need to be very strong to watch them suffer after ingestion. It’s one of the worst things that I’ve experienced.” Yet it is an experience that is becoming increasingly familiar, with concern growing across East Africa in recent years over herders poisoning lions in retaliation for livestock attacks. For conservation organizations like Lion Guardians, where Kesoi serves as community manager, it is a threat to their mission statement of mitigating human-wildlife conflict to help restore depleted lion populations in the region. In a census carried out last October, the team documented 275 lions living within a roughly 3,700-square-kilometer (1,429-square-mile) expanse of the greater Amboseli-Tsavo ecosystem, equating to approximately 7.2 lions per 100 square kilometers — a meteoric rise from the estimated one lion in every 100 square kilometers when the organization launched in 2006. Roughly 177 lions were estimated to be present in a 5,341-square-kilometer (2062-square-mile) area of neighboring Tanzania’s Ngorongoro Conservation Area (NCA), according to a 2025 survey by conservation group Kope Lion, up from 120 in 2022. As their numbers rise, so does the frequency of livestock attacks and subsequent retaliation; both Lion Guardians and Kope Lion reported “significant” increases in human-lion conflicts last year. Historically, scores would be settled by way of the spear, often wielded by Maasai warriors in revenge parties or participating in ritual killings — known as “Ala-mayo.” Now, attitudes have changed, with most Lion Guardians staff drawn from local Maasai communities. Only two lions were killed in retaliatory hunts in Amboseli-Tsavo in 2025, according to Lion Guardians. Over the last few years, a new weapon has been used, one that’s harder to detect and more devastating. On January 7, six lions were found dead by poisoning near the Kenya-Tanzania border, two days after another six — an entire pride — were killed via the same means inside the Amboseli ecosystem. Last month, 10 lions were discovered dead in the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. Though the investigation is not complete, preliminary findings suggest they ingested poison, according to the Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority. Each report is a bitter pill to swallow for Kesoi. “We [Maasai] regard poison as a cowardly act,” he said. “That is a recent development.” The silent killer The killing method is simple: finding slain livestock, herders lace the carcass with poison, which lions ingest upon returning to feast. Sometimes, livestock are not involved at all, with Kesoi recalling one incident where lions had been struck down after feeding on a poisoned giraffe. Substances used can vary. While bright blue insecticide carbofuran (sold under the name Furadan) has historically been the dominant choice, odorless pesticide strychnine has recently begun to appear, says Kesoi. Both are heavily restricted in Kenya and Tanzania, though black-market channels and smuggling via porous routes between the two countries’ borders have allowed herders to get their hands on the highly toxic chemicals. Once ingested by lions, the pain follows quickly. Detoxification is frequently successful if administered swiftly. Kesoi and his team saved all but one of the nine lions poisoned by eating the young calf. Yet even the region’s finest trackers cannot monitor the whole national park. Only lions documented as chronic livestock attackers are fitted with GPS collars, meaning scouting teams mostly rely on first-hand monitoring and reports that often never come. What’s more, poisoners are increasingly moving laced carcasses to remote or secluded areas, says Lion Guardians lion-monitoring coordinator Filberto Mayiani. By the time teams reach the scene, it is often too late — not just for the lions but for other species that consume the tainted meat. More than 30 dead vultures lay strewn around six of the lions fatally poisoned in January. “You’ve taken so many lives, all because you were overtaken by anger,” Mayiani said of the poisoners. “It’s inhumane and it’s very, very painful.” “They think they are just poisoning that predator that has killed their livestock, but poison does not just disappear once it is consumed,” he added. “It remains in the soil, in the grass, and once it rains, it will all be swept to the various water bodies around the people … we are connecting it to almost everything.” Herders are, understandably, often the prime suspects. In 2025, 437 lion attacks resulted in 278 livestock deaths in the NCA alone, according to Kope Lion, equating to a $40,600 loss. Financial compensation can be sought through various schemes, many of which are led by conservation organizations. The Big Life Foundation, for example, has run a Predator Compensation Fund in the Amboseli region since 2003 that pays Maasai livestock owners a chunk of livestock value lost to predators. Payments are withheld if predators are killed in response. In recent years, some have sought to adopt a more incentivized approach. Kope Lion piloted a program that saw NCA communities paid roughly $35,000 between 2020 and 2023 based on the number of individual lions observed in the region each month. Villages participating in the incentive program showed strong support, resulting in zero retaliatory lion poisonings, according to the organization. Kesoi noted that compensatory measures with punitive elements are effective: these collective penalties encouraged neighborhoods to self-police by identifying and holding the responsible individuals accountable. Yet compensation schemes are not universal and, according to some herders, not always adequate. Kesoi notes that while they are generally considered sufficient within Kenya’s Amboseli, the picture is markedly different across the border. “For the Tanzanians, they are saying ‘We don’t have [enough] compensation. When they kill our livestock, we kill them,’” said Kesoi. Antidote For Lion Guardians, the antidote lies not solely in financial recompense but, rather, drawing a connection between conservation and tangible community benefits. The organization has hired schoolteachers, contributed to school fundraisers, purchased snake antivenom, treated injured livestock and covered herders’ medical bills as part of a community benefits program that dovetails with its long-established efforts to lower livestock losses: mock hunts inspired by traditional Maasai practices, for example, drive lions away from herder territories without hurting them. Research has testified to the efficacy of this more rounded strategy. A 99% drop in Amboseli-Tsavo lion killings was recorded when Lion Guardians’ community engagement approach supplemented compensation programs, a 2014 study in the Conservation Biology journal stated, a roughly 8-12% improvement on areas that relied solely on financial recompense. The surge in poisonings, however, has led to a more tailored response. The organization launched its first Anti-Poisoning Campaign event in late 2024, gathering village communities in hotspots to outline the ripple effect of poison on wider ecosystems, human health and livelihoods. One event last April in Osewan, Kenya — an area where at least 20 lions had died due to poisoning — saw a popular Maasai singer perform a self-composed anti-poisoning song. For the first time in two decades, no poisonings were recorded in the region across the year, Lion Guardians said. A cross-border event is scheduled to take place this month in the region bordering Tanzania where the six lions were found dead in January. The paradox reflected in the data, however, is that the more successful Kesoi and his team are at restoring lion populations, the more likely the big cats are to threaten livestock and tempt the wrath of embittered herders. In short, the better they work, the more work they must do. For some, that may be cause for fatigue. For the Maasai of Lion Guardians, though, it has the opposite effect. “I’ve traveled around the world. You go to these big cities and the only place that you can see a lion is the zoo,” Mayiani said. “You can’t imagine having the next generation — our kids, our grandchildren — coming into this world and having to go 100 miles from here to see a lion. This is what pushes you, so you don’t get tired, to ensure that there is a better tomorrow for our wildlife and our communities.”

cnn.com.title: A small but powerful African nation is bringing Formula 1 back to the continent. Not everyone is celebrating
cnn.com.text: Formula One is to return to Africa for the first time in more than three decades, with Rwanda granted a 10-year contract to host a Grand Prix from the early 2030s – a deal described by F1 chief Stefano Domenicali as a “landmark” moment. For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the race offers a chance to attract more visitors and investment to the East African nation and raise its global profile. Kagame has led the country for decades, and his government has long been accused of abuses over its treatment of political opponents, journalists and other critics. The race will be branded the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, presented by Visit Rwanda, the country’s tourism-promotion brand. But while Domenicali says F1 is “showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision,” Rwanda’s use of sports to promote itself internationally has drawn criticism from human rights groups. Meanwhile, allegations of its support for M23 rebels in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have also raised questions about the image it hopes to project. From soccer sponsorships to Formula One Rwanda has spent years building its international profile through sports. Its Visit Rwanda campaign has partnered with prominent European soccer clubs, including Arsenal, Paris Saint-Germain, Atlético Madrid and Bayern Munich, though the arrangements have varied. Arsenal’s eight-season partnership ended in June 2026, while PSG’s agreement runs through 2028. Bayern shifted its deal toward youth development in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, after facing criticism over the partnership. In July, English Premier League side Aston Villa signed a multi-year Visit Rwanda sponsorship agreement reportedly worth around £20 million (roughly $26.8 million) a year. Human rights campaigners, including Amnesty International UK, have spoken out against the deal, arguing that it could improve Rwanda’s international image despite concerns about repression at home and its alleged role in the conflict in eastern DRC. Critics have described such partnerships as “sportswashing.” Hosting a Grand Prix, one of the world’s most prominent sporting events, would take that strategy beyond soccer sponsorships. The race would bring teams, corporate partners, international media and spectators to Rwanda, creating opportunities to promote tourism and attract business. The government hopes it will create jobs, develop local skills and deliver lasting economic benefits. Itamar Dubinsky, a senior lecturer in African studies and politics at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel who researches sports and politics in Africa, told CNN that hosting a race differs from paying for visibility through soccer club sponsorships. It would bring the sport’s international network directly into the country. The race is planned for a new circuit in Bugesera, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Kigali, as part of a wider development project led by the Rwanda Development Board. The circuit must be completed before the race can take place, and F1 has not announced an inaugural date. Its public announcement does not specify how the project will be financed or what returns it is expected to generate. Questions remain about the cost, potential public investment and how the venue will be used outside race weekends. The image Rwanda wants the world to see Rwanda wants to be seen as a country that attracts tourists and investors and can host major international events. But that image contrasts with criticism of the government’s human rights record. Human Rights Watch (HRW) has documented restrictions on political opposition, independent media and dissent under Kagame. In a report this month, the organization warned that the Grand Prix could put journalists and vulnerable communities at risk. Lewis Mudge, HRW’s Central Africa director, said F1 had yet to explain how it would assess the agreement’s human rights implications. “The F1 talks only about the social and economic impact of this deal but, to date, we’ve seen no language with regard to what effect this could have on the human rights outlook in Rwanda,” he told CNN. Mudge said Rwanda had barred three HRW staff members from entering the country because of their work. He also cited the organization’s documentation of authorities detaining homeless people and street vendors ahead of major events. Before an international conference in Kigali in 2021, some of the city’s poorest residents were detained in a warehouse described as a transit center until foreign visitors had left, according to HRW. The organization has urged Formula One to assess human rights risks, consult civil society and establish measurable protections for journalists covering the event. F1 has not publicly confirmed that it will adopt those recommendations. F1 defended its decision to hold the race in Rwanda, telling CNN it had a “long track record of delivering significant economic, social and cultural value to our host nations.” A spokesperson said the race could inspire the sport’s more than 100 million fans across Africa and that F1 believed sport could be “a positive force for good.” F1 also referred CNN to comments by Domenicali, its president and CEO, who highlighted the potential for tourism, investment, skills development and business growth. The organization said it had spent years searching for the right partner for its return to Africa and that several parties had expressed interest. However, F1’s announcement does not explain how potential hosts were assessed or how human rights concerns factored into Rwanda’s selection. CNN asked follow-up questions about its human rights safeguards and due diligence but has not received a response. Kate Hixon, Africa advocacy director for Amnesty International USA, said Formula One should investigate whether money it receives from Rwanda could be linked to minerals procured from abusive operations in eastern DRC. Amnesty has reported abuses against miners in areas taken over by M23 and alleged that gold and coltan are smuggled into Rwanda. Hixon urged F1 to publish its due diligence findings. “Racing fans deserve assurances that money generated from the M23’s abuses is not funding the Grand Prix,” she told CNN. CNN contacted the Rwanda Development Board and the Rwandan government spokesperson for comment but has not received a response. The war next door United Nations experts have documented Rwandan military support for M23 rebels, which have seized territory in eastern DRC. Rwanda disputes allegations about its involvement. The conflict has displaced communities and caused widespread civilian suffering. A human rights observer in the DRC, known as Healing and Rebuilding our Communities (HROC RDC), described Rwanda’s international image as mixed, with recognition for development and infrastructure alongside allegations of involvement in the conflict. It told CNN that the contrast with civilian suffering in eastern DRC had fueled frustration and called for civilian protection, transparency and accountability. That frustration was also reflected in criticism from DRC Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, who called F1’s decision to hold a Grand Prix in Rwanda “morally indefensible” and said it “would help polish the image of an authoritarian leader.” Jacques Issongo, from the Congolese civil society movement LUCHA, said Rwanda’s sporting partnerships were intended to divert attention from the conflict. “By multiplying major partnerships with global sporting giants such as F1, Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, Rwanda is creating a media and diplomatic diversion,” he told CNN. Beyond the spectacle Africa’s last Formula One World Championship race was held in South Africa in 1993. South Africa hosted 23 championship races, while Morocco held one in 1958. The 1985 South African Grand Prix took place during apartheid, and French teams Renault and Ligier did not attend amid opposition to the country’s racial policies. Formula One did not return to South Africa in 1986, as international protest over apartheid hardened. It returned in 1992 and 1993 as the apartheid regime was dismantled, but financial problems then ended the South African Grand Prix again. Since then, the high cost of hosting a Grand Prix, infrastructure requirements, and competition for a place on the calendar have blocked an African return. Rwanda now hopes to overcome those barriers, but hosting the race is only part of the challenge. Formula One may bring visibility, tourism and international prestige, but Dubinsky, the African Studies researcher, says the question is what remains after the cameras leave. If Rwanda builds an expensive circuit that sees limited use, he warned, it could become a “white elephant.” The race’s success, he said, will depend on whether it delivers lasting economic and social benefits and whether those benefits outweigh the negative attention that the deal may bring. For Mudge, the bigger concern is whether Rwanda’s pursuit of international recognition will overshadow the country’s human rights record and undermine efforts to improve it. “Rwanda is run by a government that is very protective of its global image no matter the cost,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Construction on Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch in DC could begin in just two weeks
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration told a judge Wednesday evening that construction on the president’s controversial 250-foot triumphal arch could begin in just two weeks, days after the midterm elections. The Justice Department said in Wednesday’s court filing that the National Capital Planning Commission is set to meet on November 5 and could sign off on final plans for the arch that day — and with final authorization from the Department of the Interior — “construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026.” The administration last week released final plans for the arch — one of President Donald Trump’s pet construction projects in the nation’s capital. Wednesday night’s court filing comes in one of the lawsuits seeking to stop the arch’s construction. Notably, the plans released last week excluded key features of a military complex including drones and snipers that Trump has used as justification for the much-criticized project. In the plans, the contours of the arch do not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. Trump announced in September that the arch would store large numbers of drones and function as a post for military snipers, with a large cache of ammunition. While the plans submitted last week don’t include the military components Trump described, the structure still might feature them. The massive arch would sit directly across from Arlington National Cemetery where nearly 430,000 service members, veterans and their family members are buried. Veterans suing to stop its construction argue the towering structure would break the solemnity of funerals at the cemetery, while preservationists argue it would disrupt the sightline of the row of national landmarks that includes the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington House and the Robert E. Lee Memorial. An Interior Department spokesperson told CNN over the weekend that the structure will “enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike.” The proposed arch is among several projects Trump is pursuing in an effort to remake the nation’s capital to his own personal liking, prompting legal battles from preservationists and others. The idea of the arch being needed for national security purposes mirrors an argument Trump has made for building a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood. Aleena Fayaz and Sunlen Serfaty contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Judge curbs Trump administration’s hunt for noncitizen voters in some states, citing flawed data
cnn.com.text: A federal judge has ordered the Department of Homeland Security to stop certain investigative actions in its hunt for noncitizen voters, writing that the department’s efforts rely on faulty data that includes US citizens legally allowed to vote. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order that DHS’s data alleging hundreds of thousands of possible illegal voters “is widely known to inadvertently include U.S. citizens” and “leaves citizens afraid that their name will be wrongly included in the hundreds of thousands identified for investigation.” The judge’s order specifically limits actions DHS takes in the field to investigate noncitizen voting, such as interviews, and says that DHS cannot take those actions if it believes the person they’re targeting could be a US citizen. The order — which covers California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, however, does not take effect until Friday afternoon, giving the Trump administration time to appeal. Once it goes into effect, it is set to last until after the midterm elections. DHS has been a driving force behind the administration’s efforts to bolster President Donald Trump’s unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, aggressively expanding its efforts to investigate the issue. The new ruling, though limited in scope, marks a notable pushback to the agency’s approach. CNN has reached out to DHS for comment. “This order is a serious protection: the current policy targets known naturalized citizens,” Beau Tremitiere, an attorney for Protect Democracy, a legal organization that represents the groups that brought the case, told CNN. “Those operations are prohibited. And this order should otherwise force DHS to stop presuming many others are viable targets when there are indicia of citizenship.”Martínez-Olguín wrote in her order that “at issue here is the reliance on admittedly flawed and incomplete data to create a list of individuals for HSI to interview in the months leading up to an election.”The lawsuit against the government was brought by voting rights and advocacy groups who argued that DHS’s actions have already resulted in US citizens being afraid to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, as they may be included in the sweeping, faulty lists DHS has created.“The public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, far exceed Defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens,” the judge wrote Wednesday.

cnn.com.title: Fights over loyalty to America, party and Trump dominate Michigan and Kansas Senate debates
cnn.com.text: Michigan and Kansas held some of the final major Senate debates of the 2026 midterm elections on Wednesday night. And they were a study in contrasts. The Michigan Senate debate between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers was bitterly personal and ferociously contested — as befits a contest that could decide the chamber’s majority. Each candidate had a simple task. El-Sayed, the former executive director of the Detroit Health Department, needed to pin Rogers, a former congressman, to the deeply unpopular President Donald Trump and his economy — and to assuage questions from moderates about his politics. Rogers is trying to win in a state currently run by Democrats while dragging Trump’s historically low approval ratings behind him. His only hope is to disqualify El-Sayed as an acceptable senator in the eyes of voters. The debate in Kansas was a little more genial, with less focus on Trump and plenty of focus on whether Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton would be too allied with the political left — from which he repeatedly sought to distance himself — to unseat GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. And Marshall, much more than Rogers, made a point of overtly appealing to Trump’s voters. Here are takeaways from the two crucial debates: Fierce debate over El-Sayed’s loyalty Rogers raised an extraordinary question: Is El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in Michigan, really loyal to the United States? The charge came against a backdrop of searing false claims by Trump that the Democrat is a “jihadist.” Rogers claimed El-Sayed — who would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate — was bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt, and that he had donors who supported Iran-backed extremist organizations like Hamas and Hezbollah. “If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked. “You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I’m going to tell you what: That is a risk to our national security.” El-Sayed, who has repudiated the Brotherhood, accused his opponent of a “shameful” attack. “To bring into question my commitment to the Constitution is really beneath you. I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he said. ‘Pattern of deception’ vs. ‘MAGA bingo’ Rogers also sought to play into the conceit that El-Sayed, as a progressive, is too far to the left of Michigan’s electorate, and he tried to reopen splits that were exposed between rival factions during the Democratic primary. He claimed that El-Sayed was “aligned” with the Democratic Socialists of America and wants “bigger government and more taxes.” El-Sayed describes himself as a capitalist and is not a member of the DSA, but he is supported by several members of the group, including New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who campaigned with him through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula last week. Rogers also tore at Democratic divides by appealing to disaffected supporters of El-Sayed’s defeated primary opponent. “You’re a Haley Stevens voter, and you came out of this, and you said, ‘Man, I just can’t do it. He’s too extreme’ … well, guess what, you have a home with us,” Rogers said in his closing statement. Ultimately, Rogers’ attacks on El-Sayed’s loyalties were aimed at advancing a broader argument — that the Democrat simply couldn’t be trusted — and one that implied, as Trump has, that he is not a fully authentic American. “There is, again, that whole pattern of deception,” Rogers said of El-Sayed’s claim to be in favor of strong border enforcement, using a refrain to which he frequently returned. Pushing back on El-Sayed’s denials that he wants to defund the police, Rogers claimed, “This guy has got new, false information about every 30 seconds.” El-Sayed countered multiple times that it was Rogers who was being untruthful and said he was playing a classic game of distraction practiced by Trump. He repeatedly said people should be playing “MAGA bingo” at home as they ticked off Rogers’ pre-planned buzzwords. But he warned: “When you are winning MAGA bingo, we are all losing.” The Trump factor Rogers, like every Republican candidate in the midterm elections, needs a way to separate himself from Trump’s most unpopular policies without alienating the president’s supporters, who must show up in vast numbers for him to win. He started with a complex pivot — admitting that the Michigan economy was in rough shape and that people were “hurting” but arguing that if Democrats got control of the Senate they’d make it even worse. This was a long way from Trump’s argument that Americans are living through an economic “golden age.” Rogers walked a fine line on tariffs, arguing that some were working to bring jobs home from Mexico and China, but that the trade war with Canada — a huge issue in Michigan’s border-state economy — was not well thought through. Rogers argued that Democratic control of Congress would cause higher taxes and higher costs, including for gasoline. El-Sayed had an easier task given huge public dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the economy; he claimed Rogers and the president stood “hip to hip.” He said that voters should send him to the Senate to ensure “money is going to be spent on you and your kids, rather than dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” He narrowed in on Rogers’ biggest vulnerability after the Republican said all his opponent did was say “Donald Trump” over and over again. El-Sayed countered by blaming the president’s decision to go to war with Iran for making the cost of living worse. “Yes, I am going to blame Donald Trump because this is Donald Trump’s economy. We are living in it,” El-Sayed said. “We are paying more for gas, more for groceries, defunding the Department of Education.” “We need to turn the page on Donald Trump, but that means we need to stand up to Donald Trump.” Kansas debate was more about Schumer than Trump Several states away, another Democratic Senate candidate was taking a very different approach. In red Kansas — a state Trump carried by 16 points — the name of the game for Hamilton was less about tying his opponent to Trump than assuring he’d be a candidate from the political middle. In fact, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer earned more mentions than Trump, as Marshall repeatedly sought to pitch Hamilton as enabling and supporting the New York Democrat’s agenda. When asked how he differed from the Democratic Party, Hamilton said former President Joe Biden’s border policies were a “disaster” and that he’s “not somebody who favors the Socialist Party.” He said he didn’t support Medicare for All or the Green New Deal, though he liked “parts” of the latter. “We’ve heard Chuck Schumer mentioned, I don’t know, 50 times? … Maybe 20 times so far,” Hamilton said. “I find that interesting. I’ve already said I wouldn’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats [were] to control the Senate.” On the other side, Marshall distanced himself from Trump far less than Rogers has in Michigan. In fact, Marshall mostly bear-hugged Trump. When asked about Trump being unpopular even in Kansas, Marshall turned his response into an appeal to Trump supporters. “I’ve had multiple times when I’ve objected to the president before, but I do want to emphasize: We need the Trump voters to come out,” Marshall said. “And that would be my appeal tonight to people: If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes … you need to come out, because we delivered on those things.” He also said later in the debate that Trump’s “tariffs are working.” When pressed again in his differences with Trump, he said he disagreed with ICE’s tactics in southwest Kansas — which many local Republicans recently objected to — and Trump’s plan to import beef. ICE was the big issue — and it got a little personal The ICE issue made for some of the most interesting portions of the debate, with Hamilton clearly seeking to turn it to his advantage. Marshall pitched the topic as an example of his ability to get Trump and his administration on the phone when he disagrees with something that’s happening. “The first thing I did when I saw what was going on in southwest Kansas (with ICE raids), I picked up the phone, called (Homeland Security) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and said, ‘Hey, I don’t think this is quite right. What’s going on?’” Marshall said. Marshall also signaled that there could be a broader conversation about immigration reform now that the border is more secure. He noted he has delivered many babies to undocumented parents. Hamilton pounced on that remark to cast the deportations that are currently taking place as heartless. “With all of those undocumented children that you delivered, did you also call ICE and ask them to be taken away?” Hamilton said. “What did you do with these people? You had compassion for them in delivering these children, but then you support quotas.” He said when he was in Hutchinson, Kansas, “There was a preschool teacher arrested in front of her children. That’s just not OK. We militarized and politicized ICE as opposed to them doing the important job they’re supposed to do, and that is protecting Americans from dangerous, dangerous people.” This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Midterms and Iran: Congress could change hands, but Trump would still control the war
cnn.com.text: On January 10, 2007, President George W. Bush announced a surge of tens of thousands of additional troops to Iraq — among the least popular decisions of his presidency. As a senior adviser, I watched from National Security Adviser Stephen Hadley’s West Wing office. Hadley had ordered pizza, and a small group of us gathered around his television. When Bush finished speaking, Hadley began flipping through channels to gauge the reaction. Sen. Dick Durbin was delivering the official Democratic response. “Escalation of this war is not the change the American people called for in the last election,” he declared. Sen. Barack Obama was next. He pledged to “actively oppose the president’s proposal.” Hadley turned off the television. “This’ll be a fight,” he said. The next morning, traveling with Bush to Fort Benning, Georgia, I reviewed the press coverage. Republican Sen. Chuck Hagel called the surge “the most dangerous foreign policy blunder in this country since Vietnam.” Democrats had just swept both houses of Congress in the 2006 midterm elections, an outcome Bush himself called a “thumping,” driven largely by public opposition to the Iraq War. The message from voters seemed clear. Bush defied it. Over the coming months, he fired his secretary of defense; appointed new generals; a new ambassador to Iraq; and most importantly, approved a new strategy to double-down on a war that much of Washington had written off as lost. Bush later wrote that it was among the most difficult decisions of his presidency. The surge dramatically reduced violence and stabilized Iraq, giving it a chance to survive. Congress sought to reverse it with timetables to withdraw US forces and even cut funding from US troops. Bush vetoed such measures, and Congress lacked the votes to override him. The politics in Washington may have changed, but Congress was not in the chain of command, and the commander in chief determined the course and conduct of an ongoing war. A lesson for Iran Iran apparently believes that the November 3 midterm elections will determine its fortunes in the ongoing war with the US. According to a Washington Post report published Monday, Iranian officials are escalating attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to raise energy prices, punish American consumers and weaken Trump and the Republican Party before the midterm elections. An Arab diplomat described Tehran as “obsessed” with the elections. Iranian state television has tracked Trump’s approval ratings and speculated that Republican losses will constrain the war and force concessions to Iran. But Iran may discover that weakening an American president politically is not the same as constraining him strategically. Congress has powers over war and peace, including authority over military spending. But using those powers to force a determined president to change course is another matter. A president can veto legislation restricting military operations, and Congress needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override that veto. Even if Democrats win a wave election in November, they will almost certainly lack those kind of numbers. Legislators are also reluctant to cut off funding for American forces already in harm’s way. Bush is but one example. Nixon escalated the war in Vietnam in 1972 even with Democrats in the majority of both houses and opposed to the war. Clinton conducted a 78-day NATO air campaign in the Balkans in 1999, even after the House refused to authorize the operation. Obama launched extended military operations in Libya in 2011 without congressional approval. Democratic majorities in Congress would surely complicate life for Trump, bringing investigations, hearings and potentially efforts to restrict military operations. Yet Trump will remain commander in chief for another two years. And the most consequential decisions on Iran will still be made in the White House. What might Trump do? History suggests Trump will retain a relatively free hand, leaving him three broad options: First, he could pull back. Trump could declare the principal military objectives achieved, reduce operations and accept a costly accommodation with Iran to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. This may bring near-term political and economic benefits, particularly if energy prices declined. But such an outcome could leave Iran claiming victory, having survived the American military campaign and demonstrated that it could threaten international commerce to extract concessions. Iran would also be able to invest its resources to reconstitute its nuclear and missile program, undermining the stated logic of the military campaign altogether. If Trump intended to pull back for political reasons, he had every incentive to do so before the midterms. His decision to maintain the blockade despite the political costs makes a sudden retreat after November unlikely. Second, he could maintain the current strategy, but with responsive strikes. The US has blockaded Iranian ports while helping commercial vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz, increasing Gulf oil flows while imposing growing economic costs on Iran. But the strategy has produced something close to a stalemate. Iran can no longer close the Strait of Hormuz, but it continues threatening ships and regional infrastructure and imposing costs on those who use it. Meanwhile, the US believes its economic blockade will soon force Iran to make concessions at the table, including on its nuclear program. Both sides appear to believe time is on their side. Trump could seek to break this stalemate by responding more aggressively to Iranian attacks, targeting the military infrastructure that supports them. Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of US military forces in the region, previewed such an approach in September, saying, “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher cost – taking out three of yours.” The objective would be to impose clear expectations on Tehran, deter further attacks in the strait and calibrate military pressure to support negotiations and diplomacy. Tehran could escalate in response, and the conflict might widen. Even so, this approach would aim to balance military pressure and diplomacy to end the war altogether. Third, Trump could go big. Trump may decide that Iran is the defining foreign policy challenge of his second term and that he has a limited opportunity to reshape the Middle East before leaving office. That could mean expanding the campaign with Israel against Iran and its regional partners, including greater support for Saudi Arabia against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. Trump might pursue a larger objective, as well: expanding the Abraham Accords through an Israeli-Saudi agreement before his presidency ends. Such a deal was in sight shortly before Hamas’ attacks into Israel on October 7, 2023, as I describe in the first chapter of Brink, my new book on the crisis. It is not out of the realm of the possible over the next two years, and Trump will likely do all that he can to achieve such a deal. But doing so will be extraordinarily difficult. The region has changed since October 7. Saudi Arabia would need new security assurances from Washington. Israel would face difficult decisions on Gaza and agreeing to the “pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood” that’s already established in UN Security Council Resolution 2803, passed last year. Israel’s own elections later this month may determine whether this is possible. Still, presidents approaching the end of their terms often become more ambitious, not less. Whatever Trump may decide, this path — a new military campaign, tied to a diplomatic achievement — will be a tempting one. The White House clock If I was in the White House today, I’d probably advise something in the realm of the second option: maintain economic pressure, respond more forcefully to Iranian military attacks and preserve an avenue for a negotiated settlement. The objective should be a sustainable strategic outcome, with the means calibrated to achieve it. If a deal with Saudi Arabia becomes possible, pursue it — but do not assume military escalation will improve the odds. But presidents make the final decisions, not their advisers. After the midterms, Trump may feel less constrained by politics and more determined to achieve something lasting. Tehran might want to remember that history. Trump has two years left. The midterms may make him weaker politically. They could also make him more determined to settle the conflict with Iran on his terms.

cnn.com.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in New Mexico case over Cambridge Analytica scandal
cnn.com.text: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year. The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica. The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters. New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident. A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision. “Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote. After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far. The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people. New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica. Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement. Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next. Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal. Meta earnings Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter. Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday. Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month. The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter. Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year. But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. “The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

cnn.com.title: US orders departure of some embassy staff and families from Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
cnn.com.text: The US State Department ordered the departure of non-essential staff and family members at its embassy in Riyadh, a move that comes amid intensifying strikes on Saudi Arabia by the Iran allied Houthi rebels in Yemen. “The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote on X. “Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.” While the State Department is drawing down its footprint in Saudi Arabia amid escalating risks, a few other US diplomatic posts in the region are also adjusting their staffing in response to the Houthi threat, a source told CNN. “This is about the Houthis,” said a State Department official. The State Department also warned in a security alert on Wednesday that US citizens should be aware of potential attacks on airports and general travel disruptions. That message for Americans came after a series of deadly Houthi attacks in recent weeks have targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi military facilities, oil infrastructure and maritime traffic. “U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization from Chief of Mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and UAV attacks on airports in the Kingdom,” the alert said. Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have expanded operations against Houthi positions across multiple frontlines, while Saudi air power continues to provide military cover. On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted at least seven drones, including one targeting the Shaybah oil field in the kingdom’s Eastern Province, in an attack that killed two expatriate workers and injured two others. On Wednesday evening, at least one person was killed and eight others injured in an attack on the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in the country’s east, according to Saudi Arabia’s Civil Aviation Authority. The airport also sustained damage – the extent of which is still being assessed. The US has stepped up its support for the kingdom militarily by boosting intelligence and targeting support. But Saudi Arabia has been asking the US for more offensive support, and so far, President Donald Trump has decided against striking the Houthis. Earlier this month, Trump was noncommittal about possible US strikes, telling reporters the Houthi attacks were “not acceptable” and that the US “will look at” whether to join the Saudis. As Saudi Arabia finds itself increasingly under attack, other allies have also stepped up support. On Tuesday, the UK said it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Egypt also pledged “all necessary and possible forms of support” in recent days. This story has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq and Hira Humayun contributed reporting.

cnn.com.title: Pope Leo needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
cnn.com.text: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success, and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday. “The final histological reports and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery have been completed today,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, a thoracic surgery professor who led the surgical team. “The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the bulletin added. Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for roughly 40% of all cases. It’s slow-moving and often affects nonsmokers. Leo’s announcement on October 11 that he required surgery for a “nodule” on his lung came as a shock both within and outside the Vatican, given the pope’s penchant for clean living. After a short stay at a hospital in Rome, where doctors removed the lobe of his left lung, Leo returned home on October 17. The next day, he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis, leading the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace. “This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds of worshipers. Pope Leo’s recovery has beeen much faster than normal, according to Dr. Juanita Mora, the national medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, who was not part of his care team. She said doctors will monitor the pope after his recent treatment, including follow-up CT scans every three to six months for the first few years, then annually to check for any regrowth. After such surgery, patients often have respiratory physiotherapy to restore breathing capacity, Mora told CNN, adding that his affected lung should regain full function. The all-clear arrives ahead of the pontiff’s planned South America trip next month. The news that the pope had cancer complicated plans for the journey, scheduled to include stops in Peru, Uruguay and Argentina and require at least 14 flights. Though the Vatican has not officially confirmed the pope’s plans for travel, Margaritora, his surgeon, told Vatican News that he saw “no clinical reasons” for canceling the trip. If the trip goes ahead, the pontiff will probably be told to walk during his travels to prevent blood clots that can form during long flights, according to Mora. The pope, she said, should get Covid-19, flu and RSV vaccines ahead of his trip for “a little extra protection in case he were to get any of the respiratory infections.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: The increasingly brazen alleged corruption within the Trump administration
cnn.com.text: There is increasing evidence that voters are concerned about corruption ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. A CNN poll on Wednesday showed 19% of registered voters say it’s their top issue — behind only a combination of the economy and the cost of living. And two weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration is suddenly inundating them with rather vivid stories of alleged corruption. Indeed, while the corruption issue has long stalked President Donald Trump thanks to his laissez-faire approach to self-enrichment — and his explosion of wealth during his time as president — the examples of potential Trump administration corruption in recent weeks have become almost cartoonish. Just over the past month-plus, the following reports have surfaced: The grimy details That last one is the latest addition. The New York Times’ Tyler Pager reported that Alina Habba secured the $50 million employment deal with a company that had only recently been set up and doesn’t have a public profile. She also reportedly finalized the deal even as she was still serving as US attorney in New Jersey, and she began the job when she was serving as a special government employee advising then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Two weeks after she started her job, the Venezuelan banker who hired her — Julio Herrera Velutini — received his pardon, the Times reported. Habba has denied playing any role, saying in a statement to the Times, “Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the DOJ — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false.” She would not talk about her work for the company, Concord Partners. But that’s not even the only controversy involving Habba in the last seven days. Axios and the Times also reported a week ago about her allegation that fellow Trump ally Richard Grenell misallocated millions of dollars that her now-husband — wealthy Turkish investor Turhan Mildon — had intended as a donation for the Kennedy Center. That money was reportedly wired to a Texas defense and security equipment company for which Grenell says he formerly consulted. Mildon has extensive business interests in Venezuela, and the Times reported he has produced a text message in which Grenell allegedly said he wanted to make Mildon the “American face down in V,” referring to Venezuela. Grenell has called the allegations absurd, telling the Times: “I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him.” Trump Jr.’s wedding has led to a backlash even among congressional Republicans, some of whom want the issue probed. One senator labeled it “corruption.” Trump Jr.’s wife has said the oligarch, Umar Kremlev, is a “dear friend.” But when ProPublica first reported on the controversy, a spokesman for Trump Jr.’s brother, Eric Trump, said that he had “absolutely no clue who this person is, nor has never heard his name.” The airplanes purchased from a donor to now-former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem have led both her camp and current Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to downplay their roles and point the finger at each other. Mullin’s camp said “these planes were purchased prior to Secretary Mullin’s arrival at DHS.” Noem’s statement emphasized “the purchase was finalized under Secretary Mullin’s leadership.” And the saga involving now-former Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle led Trump to fire her. It involved not just covertly seeking $100,000 from a man seeking favors from the administration — which the man, Eric Deters, has been happy to talk about publicly — but also some eyebrow-raising messages. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” Guilfoyle allegedly wrote at one point in the Signal messages. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” read another. “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” read yet another. Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump Jr., has disputed the allegations, calling them “false” and saying, “I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” Corruption is a major issue in polls — but doesn’t necessarily strongly favor Dems These aren’t the only remarkable and eye-catching developments for those looking out for corruption over the last two years, of course. Trump has made more than $1 billion off cryptocurrency. He’s repeatedly promoted companies shortly after buying their stock, according to a CNN investigation. His social media company is allowing Wall Street firms to pay for quicker access to market-moving posts. And he accepted a jet as a gift from Qatar to use as Air Force One; it is supposed to be transferred to his presidential library. But there is evidence this issue is starting to gain traction of late. That doesn’t mean it will be a huge liability for Trump and the GOP, but it’s certainly something to watch. A Gallup poll recently showed a record-high 89% of Americans said corruption was widespread in the US government. In addition to the CNN poll showing 19% of registered voters said it was their top issue, a recent Fox News poll showed 88% of registered voters said they were “extremely” (60%) or “very” (28%) concerned about corruption in government. Those numbers rival 2006, at the height of the sprawling Jack Abramoff lobbying scandal. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of corruption 62%-29%. And a Washington Post/ABC News poll showed nearly two-thirds of Americans said Trump was using the presidency to enrich himself. One point in the GOP’s favor here: There is also evidence that the issue might not favor Democrats as much as they’d hope. The CNN poll showed registered voters favored the Democratic Party on the issue by 7 points, 33%-26%. And a New York Times/Siena College poll shows likely voters favor the Democrats, 50%-39%. But the Reuters-Ipsos poll showed a virtual tie, with 31% favoring both parties, and nearly 4 in 10 registered voters picking neither side. And while a recent NBC News poll showed a slight majority of Americans (52%) said the Trump administration was “more corrupt” than previous administrations, just 25% said corruption was generally more of a problem in the Republican Party than the Democratic Party. And 56% said it was “equally” a problem in both parties. In other words, the numbers don’t clearly illustrate how this issue will play in the election in two weeks. But the Trump administration seemingly can’t stop giving Democrats more material to work with.

cnn.com.title: Top Georgia election officials clash over Trump-fueled conspiracy theories
cnn.com.text: On his nationwide campaign swing for Republicans, President Donald Trump traveled to Dalton, the self-proclaimed “Carpet Capital of the World,” last week and revived a familiar falsehood: that Georgia’s past elections were rigged. In the rural manufacturing hub, democracy was humming. More than 900 people streamed through the Whitfield County courthouse — far and away the county’s busiest day in the first week of early voting. And in this deep-red part of northwest Georgia, the official overseeing those ballots had a sharply different message. Whitfield County Election Director Shaynee Bryson told CNN that Georgia elections are secure, calling Trump’s claims “discouraging.” “We do try to overlook it because we know the truth,” Bryson said. “And the majority of our voters know the truth.” Election distrust has taken root here since 2020, as it has in many parts of red-leaning America. Bryson, who identifies with neither party, has spent election after election batting down false claims and conspiracy theories. “I’ll say, ‘You know I agree with a lot of points that you agree on as well. Why would I ever rig it to be a different way for another candidate to win?’” she said. Bryson fears election tensions are boiling up again. Her staff has started opening mail with gloves and masks after letters containing suspicious white substances arrived this month at election and political offices across the country, including in Georgia. “I worry about Election Day workers at times,” Bryson said, “That’s what keeps me up at night. What if? What if?” Few states carry more political scar tissue from 2020 than Georgia. Trump and his allies made it a centerpiece of their effort to challenge — and overturn — his defeat. That campaign included Trump’s infamous call urging Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to reverse the result. Since then, the Trump-aligned Georgia State Election Board has become a more powerful and combative force in an “election integrity” campaign. It has pushed tighter voting rules while raising doubts about voting systems and election results. The board has also repeatedly attacked Raffensperger, portraying him as either incapable of running Georgia’s elections or unwilling to do so honestly. Late last month, the board sent a letter to the Justice Department, asking the Trump administration for “intervention” in Georgia’s elections over its voting systems and machines. The request has fueled fears that Trump — who has sought greater federal control over elections — could take aggressive steps affecting the midterms in one of the country’s most closely watched battlegrounds. Trump and his allies’ actions denying Georgia’s 2020 results became a central piece of racketeering charges against him and over a dozen of his supporters. After years of investigations, grand juries, court maneuverings, and a wild Fulton County mug shot, the case eventually crumbled before moving ahead or going to trial due to a botched prosecution. The FBI served a search warrant to the Fulton County election warehouse outside Atlanta in January, taking roughly 700 boxes of election material to probe alleged vote fraud in the 2020 presidential election. The effort, fueled in part by 2020 election skeptics, drew sharp criticism from Raffensperger and other officials from both parties. “Worst possible scenario: Election Day, before the votes are counted, they come in, confiscate the ballots, take them off,” Fulton County Chairman Robb Pitts told CNN. “What I’ve learned with this administration, the impossible is always possible. We’re prepared though.” There are also concerns — even in Republican-leaning areas — about possible federal action in the election. In Cherokee County, the director of elections made a supplemental presentation for poll workers on what to do if federal agents come to polling locations. An election board invites Trump in On September 30, Georgia State Election Board Executive Director James Mills sent a formal request to federal officials seeking Justice Department involvement in a series of election-related concerns. The five-page letter, addressed to US Attorney General Todd Blanche, Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, asked federal authorities to investigate Georgia’s voting system, review software updates for Dominion voting equipment, examine alleged security and ballot-secrecy vulnerabilities and preserve election records under federal supervision. Mills did not respond to CNN’s questions or request for comment about the letter. This latest chapter of political fallout from 2020 is part of a yearslong struggle between Georgia’s five-member State Election Board, which writes election rules and investigates alleged violations, and Raffensperger, whose office has been tasked with administering elections statewide since January 2019. Republican Janelle King, who joined the board in 2024, argues Georgia’s voting system remains out of compliance with state law. She points to concerns that voters cannot independently verify QR codes printed on ballots and raises broader questions about ballot security and secrecy. “The system itself has proven that there are vulnerabilities, whether they were exploited or not, that’s obviously up for debate,” King told CNN. She argues that the board’s letter to the Department of Justice is justified and that its intervention is badly needed. “It’s basically letting the secretary of state know that as the State Election Board, we are aware that Georgia’s elections are not in compliance,” King told CNN. “So we want you to fix this. And the fact that you’re not listening to us, you’re not listening to the people, maybe you will listen to the DOJ.” King said she looks forward to working with “new blood” in the next secretary of state, regardless of their party affiliation, now that Raffensperger’s second four-year term is coming to an end. But other current and former officials are eager to defend the state’s efforts. “It’s obviously safe to vote in Georgia; our systems are secure,” said Gabe Sterling, who recently left his position as Georgia’s top voting manager, where he had been Raffensperger’s right-hand man since 2019. “We have fantastic professionals who run county offices, and that’s where the rubber meets the road, Sterling told CNN. The longtime Republican, who spent years as the chief operating officer in the secretary of state’s office and is now a senior fellow with Secure Democracy USA, said he has “very few actual real concerns” that Georgia’s voting systems could be tampered with, but does worry about potential online meddling from outside bad actors. “The Russians, the Iranians, the Chinese continue to do those same things in social media, emails, websites to try to exacerbate difficulties and exacerbate belief and outcomes,” he said. Sterling witnessed firsthand that dangerous rhetoric can lead to threats made to election officials, and said he’s thankful that the state election board Republican members “have no real power” and have been smacked down by the Georgia Supreme Court as well as fined for violating open records acts. “They are just bad actors,” Sterling stressed, adding that the executive director “is now just going completely off the rails.” Critics warn of eroding public trust Secretary of state officials and the board’s Democratic member echo Sterling, saying the latest effort is less about election security than sowing doubt about election results. “We have the most accurate election in the entire country,” Raffensperger told CNN in an interview in his office. He strongly pushed back on the claims in the election board letter, saying that it “wasn’t supported by the facts.” “We’re going to make sure that we have free, fair, and fast elections,” Raffensperger said, “the voters trust the process that we have here in Georgia.” Raffensperger, who lost the Republican primary for Georgia governor this year and will leave office in January, was not concerned about the possibility of federal interference and noted that his office has been a “great partner” to the Department of Justice. Democratic board member Sara Tindall Ghazal told CNN that the board has become “a platform for wild conspiracy theorists.” Ghazal called Mills’ letter a “predictable bad-faith effort to undermine confidence in our election and lay the groundwork to contest election results they do not like.” Last May, the election board gave Trump’s Justice Department a blueprint for obtaining a criminal search warrant for its Fulton County raid. The Justice Department, using a grand jury, also demanded details about thousands of election workers who assisted Fulton County in the 2020 vote-counting. Those investigations are ongoing. In a recent interview on CBS’ “60 Minutes,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon defended the Trump administration’s election related investigation. Dhillon said that “absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states.” Who ultimately oversees Georgia’s elections? At the center of the dispute is a fundamental question that is likely to persist beyond November: How much authority should the State Election Board wield compared with the independently elected secretary of state? And will DOJ try to insert itself? The board has five voting members: a chairman appointed by the governor; one member appointed by the state Senate; one member appointed by the state House; and two members selected by state political parties, one Democrat and one Republican. Since Mills was appointed to the executive director job in 2025, he has repeatedly clashed with the board’s chairman, John Fervier. Fervier, a vice president of risk management at Waffle House, was appointed by Republican Gov. Brian Kemp in 2024, but often finds himself voting alongside Ghazal, the board’s lone Democrat. The latest controversy comes as Georgia voters prepare to elect a new secretary of state, who will inherit responsibility for managing elections and navigating the increasingly tense relationship with the election board. Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds, a former Fulton County judge who also served in a federal civil rights role during the Biden administration, says the state’s elections have become a target of politically motivated attacks. “This is the state of Congressman John Lewis and Martin Luther King Jr. and so many of our civil rights leaders who marched and protested and died for the right to vote,” Reynolds told CNN. She said many of the current disputes are driven by “fear tactics” that are “built on fear and confusion.” Her Republican opponent, state Rep. Tim Fleming, is a former deputy secretary of state and chief of staff to Kemp. Fleming has campaigned heavily on his experience managing state government operations and argues he is best positioned to succeed Raffensperger. Fleming did not respond to CNN’s requests for an interview. The Republican has championed voter ID requirements, hand-marked paper ballots and other election-integrity measures. Reynolds said she supports continuing Georgia’s use of voting machines while also exploring broader use of hand-marked paper ballots. If elected, she pledged to defend voting rights against what she describes as ongoing efforts to undermine public confidence in elections. “What Raffensperger did in standing up with regard to that telephone call and standing up to the unfounded claims that somehow the election was not free, fair, and secure, and legal … because he would not do the bidding of his Republican colleagues, they retaliated,” Reynolds told CNN. And if she wins her race, “I’ll have my hands full,” she said.

cnn.com.title: Where Trump sees a deal, Putin sees a win for Russia
cnn.com.text: If only Donald Trump were President of Russia, he would surely agree a quick and easy deal to end the brutal Ukraine war, even – he might suggest – in as little as 24 hours. It is, from Trump’s point of view, a no-brainer. Not only would a resolution to the grinding conflict, now in its fifth year, halt the killing of what Trump refers to as the thousands of “young, beautiful kids” being slaughtered every month on the front lines, but it would – crucially – also be immensely profitable. Sanctions on Moscow could be swept away while lucrative trade deals would inevitably ensue. Peace and prosperity, in other words, would prevail. But, of course, Trump is not the President of Russia. That would be President Vladimir Putin, and the actual Kremlin strongman appears to have very little interest in compromising his stated war aims in Ukraine, either for the sake of Russian and Ukrainian lives or even for billions of dollars more in his state coffers. It is a fundamental misunderstanding that has driven the Trump administration’s fruitless efforts to broker an end to the fighting, and which was again on show during the latest critical meeting in St. Petersburg between Trump’s business buddy-turned-top negotiator, Steve Witkoff, and Putin himself. At the table, Putin told Witkoff he was “curious” about the outcome of meetings in Norway the day before, where officials from the US, Europe and NATO huddled with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine to hammer out new potential peace proposals, including economic incentives for Moscow. Later, a top Kremlin aide confirmed Trump’s envoy briefed the Russian leader on the discussions, before adding, inevitably, that “in truth, these contained little of actual value for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.” It was an entirely predictable outcome from a Kremlin that has stubbornly refused to budge from its hardline positions, including gaining control over the entire Donbas region of eastern Ukraine and a say in Kyiv’s future security arrangements. Still, the White House may have genuinely hoped the Kremlin would show more willingness to compromise, especially after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports last week – a politically-driven bid to ease fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, but also a huge economic boon for Moscow. Later, Trump announced an (unsuccessful) energy ceasefire that would have compelled Ukraine to halt damaging drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Amid the recriminations, during which US intelligence sharing was impacted, Trump also called for a change in the Ukrainian leadership – all music to the Kremlin’s ears. For Moscow, though, the deals, the incentives, and even the shared disdain for Kyiv are not seen as a cue to play ball and back down, but as a sign that its US strategy is yielding results. And that strategy, unlike Washington’s, is clear-eyed, with the Kremlin leader understanding what motivates Trump and effortlessly distracting his temperamental opposite number in the White House with the promise of vast economic deals. More of those were tabled by the Kremlin at the Witkoff meeting in St. Petersburg, where Putin praised the controversial diesel deal before suggesting Russia could also step up exports of crucial fertilizers to the US, and much more. “We are also discussing different projects such as data centers, projects in energy and energy cooperation,” Kiril Dmitriev, the head of the Russian sovereign wealth fund and a key Kremlin interlocutor with Trump administration officials, said after the three-hour-long talks broke up. And it’s not just economic baubles that the Kremlin uses to flatter and charm, or to keep a sympathetic ear at the White House. Putin’s release – ahead of the St. Petersburg meeting – of a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, held by Russia since being captured in Ukraine in 2022, at the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion, was cast by a fawning Witkoff as the act of “a humanitarian.” Hubbard, originally from Michigan, is reported to have suffered acute health problems during his four long years of captivity in a remote Russian penal colony. But his eventual release was lauded by the White House as a sign of Trump’s deal-making prowess and Putin’s deference. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia,” read a statement posted on Trump’s own Truth Social platform. But it’s unlikely the tough former KGB officer in the Kremlin sees it that way.

cnn.com.title: New Mexico attorney general files civil lawsuit against two Epstein advisers
cnn.com.text: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against two of Jeffrey Epstein’s closest advisers, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes. The advisers, Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn, have faced scrutiny over their ties to the late sex offender since the Justice Department released files related to Epstein late last year. Indyke, a longtime Epstein employee and attorney, and Kahn, Epstein’s longtime accountant, are the co-executors of Epstein’s estate. Earlier this year, Torrez’s office began investigating the property Epstein owned in the state, known as Zorro Ranch, after allegations about it were included in the files. The two advisers have denied any knowledge of or involvement in Epstein’s sex trafficking operation. Torrez told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Wednesday that Indyke and Kahn are “going to have every opportunity to come here to the state of New Mexico, appear before a jury, and explain to them exactly what they knew, when they knew it, and what involvement and what role they played in the enterprise that facilitated Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.” Torrez said during a news conference on Wednesday that the civil lawsuit aims to prevent Indyke and Kahn from getting any money from Epstein’s trust.
