CNN has previously reported that as part of Epstein’s will, Indyke was left with $50 million and Kahn was left $25 million. “Frankly, if anyone is entitled to a recovery of Jeffrey Epstein’s estate, it’s the survivors,” Torrez said, adding, “There should be no distribution of Mr. Epstein’s remaining assets to people like Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn for participation in what I think is one of the most horrific criminal enterprises in modern American history.” In a statement, Daniel Weiner, a lawyer for Indyke and Kahn, said they “emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General’s allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present.” Indyke and Kahn said during their congressional depositions that they haven’t received any money for their work overseeing the estate. Attorneys for the two previously told CNN that any fee or any bequests from the trust would come only after the estate’s creditors and claimants have been compensated and after the probate is concluded. The lawsuit alleges that given Indyke and Kahn’s roles as lawyer and accountant, respectively, they were “enmeshed” in the criminal activity and had “personal involvement in countless transactions that facilitated the trafficking and sexual abuse.” It goes on to accuse the two of receiving several benefits for “remaining silent” about Epstein’s crimes, including their salaries, gifts and becoming beneficiaries of Epstein’s estate. Weiner questioned the thoroughness of the state attorney general’s investigation, saying no one from that office reached out to speak with Indyke or Kahn, and noting that they “have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so.” Wednesday’s civil lawsuit comes as Indyke and Kahn are also reportedly under federal investigation. They have additionally faced multiple lawsuits from survivors for compensation. In February, Torrez reopened New Mexico’s criminal investigation into Zorro Ranch after the files released by DOJ included a 2019 email received by a local radio host that alleged that “somewhere in the hills outside the Zorro, two foreign girls were buried on orders of Jeffrey and Madam G.” As part of the probe, New Mexico authorities have searched the property. Torrez has also filed a lawsuit against DOJ and US Attorney General Todd Blanche, accusing the department of “hiding information about Epstein and his co-conspirators” and “stonewalling” the state’s investigation. An Epstein survivor who has been to his Zorro Ranch told CNN she’s “grateful” for the state attorney general’s efforts. “Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn know the truth, and so do we,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous to protect her privacy. “I’m ready and willing to help this truth come to light.” Separately, a bipartisan commission of New Mexico lawmakers are also looking into the allegations of criminal activity surrounding Zorro Ranch and have issued multiple subpoenas, though not to Indyke and Kahn. Earlier this year, Indyke and Kahn sat for closed-door depositions with the House Oversight Committee, during which they said that they were unaware of Epstein’s crimes, despite having worked for Epstein for decades and being intimately involved in Epstein’s business dealings and finances. “Let me be clear: I had no knowledge whatsoever of Jeffrey Epstein’s wrongdoings,” said Indyke, who began working for Epstein in 1996, during the March deposition. “My complete lack of involvement in that misconduct is a matter of record. Not a single woman has ever accused me of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, or claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to me any allegation of Mr. Epstein’s abuse.” Meanwhile, Kahn, who began working for Epstein in 2005 and said he only saw him approximately every three weeks, then told lawmakers, “We did not interact socially, and I never attended any of his parties or his social functions. While Epstein was alive, I never observed any sexual abuse or trafficking of women and never received a complaint — either by one of Epstein’s victims or anyone else — of such abuse or trafficking.” Both men also said during the depositions that if they had known about Epstein’s trafficking of women and girls while working for him, they would have cut ties with him immediately. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Global websites shut down after AI found a critical flaw affecting 70% of the internet
cnn.com.text: Several government and company websites around the world went dark briefly on Wednesday, after artificial intelligence helped discover and address critical bugs that could affect 70% of the internet. The vulnerabilities were uncovered by teams at OpenAI, Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif. The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to execute code and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. AI played a crucial role in Wednesday’s discovery, allowing researchers to conduct cybersecurity work across multiple apps in just hours, the companies said. The disclosure comes after advancements in AI have raised concerns from Washington to Silicon Valley about how the technology could supercharge cyberattacks. “With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process. The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public on Wednesday after PHP had a fix for it. The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language PHP that is at the center of the vulnerability, has released a patch for the bugs and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately. The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue. The National Security Agency in a social media post urged organizations using PHP to update their systems, or take them offline if they’re unable to do so. The disclosure prompted some government websites in Europe to go offline as companies updated their systems, according to Reuters. Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected. Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: State Department warns Americans about Latin America. Privately, it tells asylum officers a different story
cnn.com.text: The State Department is publicly warning Americans about violent crime in parts of Latin America, but privately, it has given asylum officers new assessments arguing that conditions in some of those same countries are no more dangerous than in some US cities, according to internal documents reviewed by CNN. The documents, which have not been previously reported, focus on Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador. Rather than emphasizing human rights issues and the prevalence of kidnapping and extortion often highlighted in State Department assessments, they instead compare violent-crime rates in those countries favorably with US cities such as Baltimore, Houston and Memphis. The new assessments are part of a broader Trump administration effort to overhaul the way claims from migrants are assessed by asylum officers — and limit who’s eligible to remain in the United States. Asylum applicants must prove they are unable or unwilling to return to their home country because of a “well-founded fear” of persecution. By lowering the perceived threats in those countries, the new assessments will likely bear directly on those claims, including determinations of whether migrants can safely relocate inside their own country rather than seeking to stay in the US. “There’s been an oversimplification of real dangers in these countries during other administrations, but this seems to be going too far in the other direction,” said Andrew Selee, president of the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan thinktank. The State Department says the assessments were prepared by personnel with regional expertise and circulated for review, including to US missions overseas. They are “intended to provide background for adjudicators as they evaluate protection claims,” one document states. The Department of Homeland Security, which manages asylum claims, referred CNN’s questions about the country reports to the State Department. In a written statement to CNN, a State Department spokesman said the department “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries to (US Citizenship and Immigration Services) and immigration courts. Such information is intended to provide useful background for USCIS personnel and immigration judges.” A new yardstick for asylum claims The new documents were distributed to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the agency inside DHS that processes immigration benefits, and state that violent crime in Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador is lower than in some major US cities. In Mexico and El Salvador, for example, the documents claim that many areas “have violent crime rates at least one order of magnitude lower than those of major US cities.” Asylum officers generally rely on the State Department’s annual human rights report to assess conditions in an applicant’s home country. That report, which covers the prior year and is usually released in March or April, has been delayed this year. The new assessments therefore give officers more recent country conditions to consider when reviewing claims. Asylum denials are already high. In June, for example, 94% of asylum cases were denied, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. That’s a dramatic increase from two years ago when the asylum denial rate hovered around 50%. The documents show how the Trump administration is using comparisons with the US to evaluate two questions that can determine an asylum claim: whether a home government can provide protection and whether an applicant could safely relocate within the country. “When you see a government report differ so much from previous reports, it raises red flags, especially if conditions on the ground haven’t changed in a noticeable way that would warrant that,” Selee said. “Some change is OK. You can correct the emphasis in prior reports, but this seems like a wholesale shift in conditions on the ground.” The State Department warns against travel to Honduras, citing violent crime and terrorism, according to an alert on its website. It specifically cites Gracias a Dios Department, a region in Honduras, for its crime. The State Department’s public travel warning cites crime in the region. The internal documents, however, say violent-crime rates there and in other Honduran cities “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in parts of the United States,” including Baltimore, Houston and Memphis. “Of course, these figures do not represent the entirety of the United States,” the document states in one part. “Rather, they demonstrate that, even in developed countries, conditions vary. Further, they demonstrate why a general judgement cannot be made concerning a country’s conditions based on conditions in certain areas.” Can asylum seekers safely relocate? The documents also assert that police in Honduras are “willing to and able to respond to requests for assistance from residents, with the main constraints being vehicle storages, response-time challenges, and uneven rural access.” That, too, it states can happen in the United States. But the realities on the ground are more complicated, Selee said. “That clearly understates the degree to which police forces are in collusion with organized crime groups,” Selee said. “The difference with the United States is that often people face violence but no trustworthy institutions that can protect them.” The new documents state that people can move freely in each of the countries. That includes victims of abuse and extortion. While experts say that may be the case, they note that some organized crime groups can pose a threat across the country, meaning that even by relocating, people remain in potential danger. “The reality is that there are some people who fall afoul of criminal groups and cannot be safe anywhere in the country,” Selee said. Former USCIS officials said that determining whether someone can relocate in country has been part of the regular line of questioning by asylum officers. “The question of whether you can relocate in your own country has always been something an officer can and should consider,” a former USCIS official told CNN. Trump officials have repeatedly said that travel warnings, which are separate from the State Department’s human rights reports, are intended for US citizens and not nationals of that country. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, speaking to CNN’s Jake Tapper in June, defended the administration’s policies when asked about the safety of Haiti, which also has a travel warning. “We have ‘Do not travel’ in places in Mexico or advisory warnings. In fact, if you go through our website in the State Department, you’ll see there’s advisories to a lot of places that are vacation destinations that we have advisories on because of the real risk to Americans,” said Mullin. “That doesn’t mean it’s a risk to people who live there,” he added.

cnn.com.title: Supreme Court hands Trump a rare loss on transgender prison care policy
cnn.com.text: The Supreme Court on Wednesday blocked President Donald Trump from suspending hormone therapy and other treatments for transgender Americans in federal prisons, a rare win for transgender rights at the conservative high court. The court handed down a one-sentence order that did not explain the decision. “This is a critical ruling for our clients and all transgender people in Bureau of Prisons custody,” said Li Nowlin-Sohl, a senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s LGBTQ & HIV Project. “The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights. We will continue to defend the rights of our clients and all incarcerated people.” The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Since Trump returned to power last year, the Supreme Court has allowed the administration to ban trans people from serving in the military and permitted a policy that requires that the sex designation on US passports align with a traveler’s sex assigned at birth. The court also this year upheld state laws that prohibit transgender athletes playing on girls’ sports teams. The latest emergency appeal hit on an issue Trump raised during his 2024 campaign with a series of television advertisements that criticized Democratic nominee Kamala Harris for her approach to trans Americans. On his first day back in the White House, Trump signed an executive order barring “any medical procedure, treatment, or drug” for the purpose of “conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” The Bureau of Prisons later implemented a policy that permits psychotherapy and psychiatry services for inmates with gender dysphoria, but not hormone therapies, surgeries or “social accommodations.” That can include items such as clothing and makeup. A US district court and a federal appeals court in Washington, DC, blocked the Trump policy from taking effect in the short term. In a brief order last month, the DC Circuit concluded that the administration’s policy was likely arbitrary and capricious because the Bureau of Prisons had not “adequately” considered “its own experience providing gender-affirming care under its prior policy.” In its emergency appeal to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that it did consider that experience and that the previous treatment and accommodations “raised security and prison-administration concerns that outweighed whatever limited benefits they had.” Three prisoners who said they had been receiving hormone therapy for years challenged the policy, arguing it was an abrupt change to decades of policy and would end treatment for nearly 1,000 people in custody. The assertion of security concerns within prisons, the American Civil Liberties Union told the Supreme Court, was odd “given that BOP has not pointed to a single security incident relating to its provision of this treatment over the past 30 years.” Two conservative justices — Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito — dissented from Wednesday’s order, but did not say why. The lack of explanation was particularly notable given that the case has been fully briefed and ripe for an order for almost two weeks. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: The future of banking: Digital trend ‘will only accelerate’ with Gen Z
cnn.com.text: Digital payments are already altering the way we shop, dine and go about our daily business. Gen Z is proving to be an eager adopter of new payment technologies. A 2025 report found that up to 91% of zoomers in the US use smartphone apps like Apple Pay, Google Pay, Venmo or PayPal. Gen Z comprises 27% of the global workforce — and their digital habits are already influencing the way businesses operate. “This trend signals a permanent shift toward digital payment methods that will only accelerate as Gen Z assumes more decision-making roles in business,” said the report by Billtrust, a fintech company that has studied usage trends over the last decade. Banks are ‘redefining’ their branches As much as Gen Z and other consumers may think they don’t need traditional banks anymore, banks are capitalizing heavily on the digital payment revolution. Many are partnering with fintech giants to stay relevant; other banks continue to evolve. “In a time when many consumers are embracing digital banking, some banks are redefining their branches, rather than being in a hurry to close them,” said Karen Bennett, a banking analyst with Bankrate. In fact, Bennett said, the US bank branch network has now “posted three consecutive quarters of net growth, which is the first stretch like that since 2009,” meaning they have added a net gain of 120 branches during that time. Traditional banks, she said, are catering to all needs, across generations, “by keeping branches around and also enhancing their digital apps.” “Consumers are now more likely to turn to apps than branches for routine banking tasks like deposits, transfers and balance checks,” Bennett said. “In turn, branches are often being repositioned around the transactions or conversations that still benefit from human contact.” That includes things like mortgages, advice on big financial decisions, opening a first savings account, and working through fraud issues on an account. The digital revolution is ‘at its frenzy’ Two big shifts are driving innovation, especially in the Middle East, said Gaurang Shah, an executive vice president of Mastercard who is focused on expanding and driving digital payment innovations and strategies. “Digital payment innovation is at its frenzy,” he said, “and the consumer demands and expectation has gone off the roof, especially after the pandemic. So, the consumer wants or expects a seamless digital first journey with embedded payments that they can trust inherently.” Shah made his comments earlier this year at the Web Summit Qatar that brought together more than 30,000 people from over 120 countries, including tech leaders, innovators and investors to discuss the Middle East’s digital ecosystem. Shah predicted that by 2030, consumers would be able to go to their favorite coffee shop — and instead of placing their order, their eyes and face would get scanned through biometrics authentication. “That’s the world we are going to be moving into,” he said. The pace of change in digital banking is evident around the Mideast and Asia where financial institutions are asking questions like: Why can’t every phone be a commerce device? What more can be done to help vendors to improve sales through digital transactions? And how can we improve the customer experience by shaving off a few more seconds at checkout? At the same Qatar conference, Ali Abulhasan, the co-founder and CEO of Tap Payments, said his contactless payment company is already processing about $200 billion in digital transactions a year in the wider Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region. “We believe in the next five years,” he said, “that’s going to be at least doubling to reach over $400 billion.” The change is seemingly everywhere in urban areas: QR codes at restaurants, tap payments at vendors and retail stores alike. Jassim Althani, a senior corporate banking relationship manager with Ahli Bank Qatar, said one of the big reasons why many Mideast and Asian countries are adapting quicker than the West is that digital finance is seen as key to growing their economies. “In the Gulf, we have strong regulation, but there’s also flexibility to support innovation,” Althani told CNN. “In parts of Europe, regulatory complexity and higher costs can make change more difficult. But it also comes down to convenience — people adopt something quickly when it makes their daily lives easier.” And the bottom line, he said, is consumers increasingly want everything done directly on their phones. “The challenge,” he said, “is making everything simple without compromising security or customer support.” The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the pace and acceptance of ditching cash for digital payments — to the point where “people are comfortable with doing things on the go.” “In five years, I expect more everyday financial services to happen through our phones, with faster transfers and easier payments across borders,” he said. “Cash will still be around, but we’ll rely on it less.” People might visit bank branches less frequently these days, he said, but banks remain more relevant than ever, for our salaries, payments, savings and financing. “Even when someone pays through a [digital] wallet, there’s often a bank supporting the transaction behind the scenes,” Althani said. “Banking is becoming less visible, but it’s still central to our daily lives.” CNN’s Yahya Salem contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Astonishing winning images from Nikon's Small World photography competition 2026
cnn.com.text: An image of ink droplets inside a printer has won first prize at the Nikon Small World photomicrography competition, which focuses on images taken through a microscope. Ole Bielfeldt, a student and experimental photographer from Germany, took the photo using an imaging rig he built himself, according to a statement from the organizers published Wednesday. Bielfeldt, who is based in Cologne, Germany, said he was inspired by the mystery of how inkjet printers transfer images onto paper so precisely. “I think it was super interesting because I didn’t know how it really worked,” Bielfeldt said in the statement. “It’s like it was magic, and I didn’t understand it, but now I do.” Bielfeldt’s work won him the 52nd edition of the competition, and Eric Flem of Nikon Instruments said that his image “embodies what makes Nikon Small World so powerful: the intersection of microscope imaging, ingenuity and artistry.” “By using a microscope objective in a different way, he transformed a familiar object into something altogether new and previously unseen,” Flem said in the statement. “It is a reminder that the microscope is not only a scientific tool but also a creative one, capable of expanding how we see and imagine the world around us.” Second place went to John-Oliver Dum for an image of a jumping spider with pollen, and third was awarded to Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery for a photo of neurons inside an expanded mouse brain. Nikon also runs the annual Small World in Motion video competition, which was embroiled in controversy this year. In mid-October, the company announced that the winner had been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules.

cnn.com.title: Macron slams ‘stupid comments’ from world leaders after Trump blames France unrest on migrants
cnn.com.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has slammed what he called “stupid comments” from some foreign leaders over protests sweeping the country, after his US counterpart Donald Trump claimed migrants were fueling the unrest. “We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said Wednesday during a tour of Arab states in the Persian Gulf region. “The fact is that all those speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country. And those people irritate me.” On Monday, Trump claimed without evidence that France was being “conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity” and “the Western civilization itself.” What started out in September as protests over the state of education and cost of living in the country has since spiraled into nationwide violence and rioting, with more than 2,000 people arrested this past weekend alone. French authorities have imposed localized curfews and promised a “massive” police presence for more protests expected Saturday, as authorities come under pressure to quell the worst flare-up of rioting in years. Asked Wednesday if he was aware of any evidence of foreign involvement in the turmoil, the French president said there is “no visible foreign interference in the events that took place.” However, Macron continued, “there has been foreign manipulation of information, which has led to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders.” Alongside Trump, Vice President JD Vance has also suggested migrants were behind the unrest. “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” he wrote Monday on X. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.” Trump referred approvingly to Vance’s comments in the Oval Office on Tuesday, while claiming that concerns about education or costs were not fueling the protests. “It’s not about education. It’s about immigration,” he said. “It’s about illegal people coming in who basically hate France. They hate the people. They hate everything.” In Europe, too, Hungarian Prime ⁠Minister Peter Magyar has linked the violence to immigration policies, also without providing evidence. On Sunday, he posted on social media: “In the face of this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.” Macron did not mention any specific foreign leaders in his news briefing Wednesday, but he did accuse leaders in both Europe and “on the other side of the Atlantic” of amplifying misinformation. “We want order, respect and progress for our country. But people mustn’t go around saying things that simply aren’t true,” he said. The French president made an unannounced visit to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday for talks with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman before departing for Paris, according to the Élysée Palace.

cnn.com.title: A Netflix reality show evokes one of history’s most controversial scientific experiments — and the man behind it
cnn.com.text:
The Stanford Prison Experiment lasted less than a week in 1971, but its claims about human nature endured for decades. Now, a new Netflix series is bringing one of psychology’s most controversial studies, and some of the biggest concerns surrounding it, back into the spotlight.
Organized by American psychologist Philip Zimbardo, the experiment involved a mock prison set up in the basement of a Stanford University building. He selected 24 male college students out of more than 70 respondents to a newspaper ad for “a psychological study of prison life” and randomly divided them into prisoners and guards. At the heart of this work was a fundamental question about good and evil.
“Zimbardo was basically trying to figure out if regular people could be willing to both give and follow orders if they were placed in a particular environment, and see what was the role of the situation at producing people’s behavior,” said Catherine Sanderson, Poler Family Professor of Psychology at Amherst College and a former student of Zimbardo’s. She was not involved with the experiment. “What he wanted to show is that normal people can do horrible things.”
The experiment, meant to last up to two weeks, rapidly got out of hand — at least according to the official narrative. Within 36 hours one of the prisoners had an apparent mental breakdown, and on the second day the inmates staged a rebellion. The guards vigorously repressed it, spraying the perpetrators with fire extinguishers, stripping them naked and locking them up in a dark closet named “the hole.”
All of this was unfolding against a backdrop of real-world unrest over prison conditions and the treatment of incarcerated people. Just weeks after the experiment ended, a prison uprising at Attica Correctional Facility in New York was thwarted with deadly force, resulting in 43 deaths. The event brought media attention to Zimbardo’s work, launching it beyond the academic realm and into the social discourse, where it has remained since.
But through the years, the profile of the Stanford Prison Experiment has dramatically changed, going from an unprecedented insight into the human psyche to a widely criticized study whose methods and conclusions have been called into question.
“Our understanding of what happened has really evolved a lot over time,” Sanderson said. “There have been not only ethical challenges posed about the study, but also about whether the behaviors occurred spontaneously, or were rather sort of instructed by Zimbardo.”
As Netflix debuts its own reimagined version of the experiment, one key question remains: Did the study reveal something fundamental about authority — or did the way it was conducted help produce the behaviors it became famous for?
‘A major problem’
Zimbardo conceived the study partly as a follow-up to famous obedience experiments conducted by American psychologist Stanley Milgram in the early 1960s. In the first of such studies, participants were told to deliver what they believed were increasingly painful electric shocks to an unseen person, for giving incorrect answers in a memory test, and 65% of participants continued to the maximum level despite hearing the person’s apparent distress.
For starters, the Stanford experiment prisoners had no idea the study would kick off with local police realistically arresting them at their homes. Upon entering the mock prison, the inmates underwent a strip-search and then had to put on loose-fitting smocks with no underwear. They wore nylon stockings over their heads, simulating shaved hair.
The guards wore uniforms and mirrored sunglasses to avoid eye contact. The study team gave them wooden batons and instructions to not physically harm the prisoners, but maintain law and order. Zimbardo acted as the prison’s superintendent, observing and recording the experiment.
As prisoners started to show evident signs of distress early on, some relatives who were allowed to visit expressed the intention of contacting lawyers to stop the study. Within the first four days, three inmates had been released after showing signs of distress.
On the fifth day, Christina Maslach, then a recent Stanford graduate in social psychology who would later marry Zimbardo, visited the prison and was horrified by what she saw. Zimbardo ended the experiment the next day.
Audio and video evidence from the experiment, as well as post-study interviews with the participants, later revealed that Zimbardo, who died in 2024, directly influenced the study’s outcome by interacting with the participants and coaching the guards, as well as preventing some inmates from leaving the mock prison when they first requested it.
“One of the hallmarks of good experimental design is that we don’t have the experimenter in charge of the study interacting with the participants,” Sanderson said. “The fact that Zimbardo was so heavily involved is a major problem, because he did have particular beliefs, expectations — one might even say goals — in conducting the study.”
But at the time, the results were well regarded and Zimbardo leaned into a newfound fame: “In the public eye, like lecturing to a large class, you are a performer and so must put on a good performance and learn from mistakes to be more effective next time,” he said in 2009 interview.
Zimbardo was a very powerful and compelling speaker, according to Sanderson. “The Stanford prison study had brought him a lot of fame, and he was very charismatic,” she said. “This sort of lure meant that people weren’t paying a lot of attention to maybe some of the details about what actually happened.”
Still, the revelations about his involvement did serve to undermine the findings about authority and human nature that Zimbardo championed.
“I think there is certainly a general view that good people can do bad things under particular circumstances, such as being anonymous, or being ordered to do so,” Sanderson said. “However, the Stanford prison study is not a good example of evidence for that.”
That skepticism reflects a broader reckoning within psychology over the reliability of study results. In 2015, an attempt to replicate 100 studies published in leading psychology journals resulted in only 36% of replications achieving statistically significant results, compared with 97% in the original studies. This “replicability crisis” has exposed flaws in how psychological research is conducted and published, including small sample sizes and pressure to produce striking results rather than robust, reproducible findings.
The first major attempt to revisit the Stanford experiment did, in fact, produce a completely different outcome. But that initial redo, commissioned by the BBC, also started by shaking up the approach.
Alternate outcome
The BBC broadcast its take on Zimbardo’s work in 2002 as a television series called “The Experiment.”
The study involved 15 male volunteers — six guards and nine prisoners — in prison built on a movie studio lot. But the guards did not become tyrannical, as in the Stanford experiment. Instead, the prisoners challenged the guards and gained the upper hand. Even more surprisingly, they later built a shared community.
According to Stephen Reicher, Bishop Wardlaw Professor of Psychology at the University of St. Andrews in England, who conducted the research along with Alex Haslam, then a psychologist at the University of Exeter, the striking difference in outcome was partly due to the fact that the guards were not coached beforehand by an authoritative figure like Zimbardo.
“Normally in an experiment you are neutral,” Reicher said. “Zimbardo actually positioned himself as head guard. In broad terms, he tells them what to do. He tells them to impose power. He tells them to make people feel helpless.”
In the BBC version, there is no such leadership: “We took seriously the notion that we should just put people in the role and see what happens. Without clear leadership, we found that the guards didn’t want to impose power, didn’t want to be brutal, and therefore they became powerless. They didn’t cohere as a group. They didn’t know what to do,” Reicher noted. “Conversely, the prisoners did cohere as a group, did have a clear sense of how to act, and actually that reversed the power relations in our study.”
The revisited experiment, although made for TV, was designed as a scientific study, Reicher said.
“We took it through a scientific ethics committee,” he added. “We designed it as we would any other study. We didn’t just film what people did, we did surveys every day. We even took hormonal data.”
However, even though the prisoners came together to create a more equal system, they could not truly control what was going on: “So they felt more and more helpless, and they became more and more attracted to a strong man, to authoritarianism,” Reicher said. “What we found was that the failure of groups to be able to control their own environment makes them attracted to authoritarian regimes, which I think is actually quite an important message given what’s going on in the world today.”
Zimbardo’s construct that a bad situation can make a good person do evil things, Reicher said, is dangerous: “When you look at examples of brutality in history, afterwards those responsible nearly always try to deny accountability. The excuse is they were only following orders, they couldn’t help it,” he said. “The explanation given by Zimbardo is not only scientifically wrong; it is socially and morally dangerous because it gives perpetrators an out.”
Theater vs. science
Questions about prisoner abuse and accountability took on renewed urgency in 2004, when photographs of US soldiers and Iraqi detainees at Abu Ghraib, a prison outside of Baghdad, shocked the world. The images prompted comparisons with the Stanford experiment and Zimbardo became a prominent commentator on the Abu Ghraib scandal, arguing that the abuses could not be understood solely as the actions of a few individuals.
Zimbardo even testified for the defense of an Abu Ghraib guard, and his observations coalesced into a 2007 book titled “The Lucifer Effect: Understanding How Good People Turn Evil,” in which he wrote, “Any deed that any human being has ever committed, however horrible, is possible for any of us — under the right or wrong situational circumstances.”
The renewed popularity of the experiment led, in 2015, to a Hollywood movie starring Billy Crudup titled “The Stanford Prison Experiment,” which included Zimbardo as a consultant and largely adheres to his own version of the events.
The fiercest critique of Zimbardo’s work showed up shortly after, in 2018, when Thibault Le Texier, a French historian and associate researcher at the Centre for European Sociology and Political Science in Paris, first published a French-language book about the experiment, then summarized it in a 2019 study titled “Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment.”
Le Texier reconstructed the experiment’s entire timeline after spending weeks analyzing archival material such as recordings and transcripts at Stanford University.
“From the very beginning, the Stanford Prison Experiment was organized and planned as a show,” Le Texier told CNN. “It was more theater than science.”
Le Texier also said that while Zimbardo admitted to giving the guards broad directions, in reality either Zimbardo or his associates instructed them very specifically about how to behave during the experiment — so much that the guards were given “a blueprint” on how to act.
“They’ll have no privacy at all, there will be constant surveillance—nothing they do will go unobserved,” Zimbardo said during a guard orientation session captured on video. “They will have no freedom of action. They can do nothing and say nothing that we don’t permit. We’ll take away their individuality in various ways.”
Zimbardo’s apparent influence dashes any hopes scientists might have of gleaning firm conclusions from the Stanford prison Experiment, Le Texier added. “The only scientific conclusion you can draw is a reminder that scientists can do really bad science,” he said.
According to Le Texier, Zimbardo intentionally made it difficult for prisoners to leave the experiment even if they asked to do so, and created uncomfortable living conditions for them: “They couldn’t read, they couldn’t watch TV, they couldn’t go to the toilets at night, they had absolutely nothing to do during the day, the conditions were harsher than even a real prison, simply because Zimbardo was scared that if the prisoners had a good time nothing would happen, and the experiment would be a failure,” Le Texier said.
In 2018, Zimbardo published a lengthy response to criticism of the experiment — including that of Le Texier — in which he defended the experiment’s methods, arguing that participants could leave and that the guards’ behavior was not scripted. Le Texier rejects the response as “bulls**t,” saying that, while it served to “praise the experiment,” it did not address his criticism specifically.
Made for TV
The frequent parallels between the experiment and theatrical productions eventually drew the attention of Stephen Scott-Bottom, a professor of contemporary theater, drama and film at the University of Manchester.
“My first interest was thinking of it as a constructed situation where people are being asked to play roles,” he said. “If you ask people to role play in a scenario, and then get a different group of people to play that scenario again, you’ll end up with completely different results, depending on the particular combination of personalities.”
Zimbardo and his colleagues, Scott-Bottoms argued, wanted to emphasize the importance of the situation, so they downplayed the importance of individual personalities.
For a study about the experiment he published in 2020, Scott-Bottoms tracked down and interviewed several of the guards and prisoners, including the inmate whose apparent breakdown, about 36 hours into the study, became one of its most famous episodes: “The first emotional breakdown that you hear about in all the documentation was faked, by a guy who was just trying to get out,” Scott-Bottoms said.
The prisoner in question, Doug Korpi, had also admitted that his agony was an act to journalist Ben Blum, who included the revelation in a broader takedown of the experiment published in 2018. Korpi wanted to leave the experiment because he wasn’t allowed to study for an upcoming graduate school admission test, and was getting worried about being unprepared.
Zimbardo’s role in the prison, Scott-Bottoms said, was focused on preventing the experiment from stagnating: “I regard him as a media artist as much as a scientist,” Scott-Bottoms said. “He was very good at finding an angle or a hook to get your attention, so that you’ll listen to the thing that he really wants to talk about, rightly or wrongly.”
Just a month after Zimbardo died in October 2024, a three-part documentary titled “The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth” premiered on the National Geographic channel. It included one of Zimbardo’s final interviews.
In the documentary, several of the guards and prisoners from the original study challenge Zimbardo’s account of the event, and refer to him as “a salesman,” “kind of a clown,” “a huckster,” while repeatedly using the word “fraud” in association with the experiment.
Dave Eshleman, who emerged in the mock prison as the most ill-tempered among the guards — earning himself the nickname “John Wayne” — goes as far as calling his role within the experiment “an acting job,” and speaks of “getting in character” before entering the prison. He says Zimbardo made it appear as though the guards were not considered to be subjects in the experiment: “If it was made clear to us that we were there to be studied, not to help study prisoners, we would have acted completely differently,” he said.
In his interview, Zimbardo responds to these accusations by saying that Eshleman and the others had to justify what they did, and the easiest way to do that is to say they were acting. They could also no longer distinguish “the improv from real sadistic impulses,” the psychologist added. The fact that everybody fell into their roles, Zimbardo said, speaks to “the validity of the experiment.”
He also made no secret about the experiment’s theatrical nature: “I thought about the experiment as an improvisational drama — the basement yard, it was the stage, the actors were prisoners and guards with different uniforms and the video camera was the audience.”
The new Netflix show “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” — which was filmed in a real prison and consists of six 45-minute episodes — is not structured like the original at all, and its creators aren’t trying to conduct a scientific experiment.
“If we were simply recreating the original experiment, that would be unconscionable,” said Jane Lipsitz, the show’s executive producer, statement. “But this is a different time, with different participants, different safeguards and, ultimately, a very different journey.”
“It felt like the right time to revisit that question with a new generation and ask whether power inevitably changes us — or whether we’re capable of resisting the roles, the rules and the systems we’re placed into. What we discovered during this process was something we never saw coming,” she added.
The producers of the Netflix show said they put “several guardrails” in place to protect participants, including psychological screenings and the ability to leave at any moment just by uttering a safe word. The 30 people — including three women — involved also make up a far more diverse group than either the original study or the BBC’s work.
The guards are split into two groups and do receive an initial training, during which they are told to “take control.” But in stark contrast with the BBC revisitation and the requirements of a scientific experiment, the Netflix show is heavily structured and introduces radical changes to its setup as it progresses — with entertaining, if unrealistic, results.
Even half a century on, there are still interesting aspects of the original Stanford experiment, despite its flaws, Reicher noted. The new show is perhaps testament to that.
“The study is still in the textbooks. There are also still people who reject it entirely. And there are others who say there are things to learn from it, specifically about the role of leadership,” Reicher said. “In the end, in any study, you don’t describe everything. You describe what you think is important.”

cnn.com.title: The iPhone Duo is Apple’s coolest phone in years. There’s just one problem
cnn.com.text: There were many times I didn’t want to put the iPhone Duo down. Once you get used to reading, watching TV and scrolling through Instagram on a giant screen, it’s hard to go back to a tiny glowing rectangle. There’s just one issue: Many apps are still made for that little rectangle. This is what it’s been like to use the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, which launches on October 23. It starts at $2,000, making it as expensive as Apple’s latest 14-inch MacBook Pro. It’s a big move for Apple, which rarely messes with the winning formula that’s turned the iPhone into a business that raked in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. But after years of incremental iPhone updates, Apple faced pressure to prove it could still captivate consumers. I got a taste of that future after spending about a week with the new foldable phone that Apple provided CNN for testing purposes. The iPhone Duo became my tablet for watching Netflix, a bedside alarm clock at night, an extra screen for watching football on Sunday, a miniature monitor when connected to my Bluetooth keyboard and a camera with a built-in tripod. But there were equally as many times – if not more – when I grew frustrated because apps didn’t work the way they should, since developers haven’t updated them yet. And despite Apple’s “it just works” approach, the iPhone Duo takes some getting used to. While the iPhone Duo’s software certainly felt much smoother and more fluid than Android alternatives, many of its core features have been available on Samsung or Google phones for years. What can iPhone Duo do that a regular phone can’t? The iPhone Duo is the biggest change Apple has made to the iPhone in its nearly 20-year history. There’s a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, which unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display on the inside. When closed, the iPhone Duo feels like a passport, but obviously thicker and heavier. When opened, it’s like a thinner and smaller iPad Mini. One of the most popular questions I get about the iPhone Duo is whether you see the crease. The answer, believe it or not, is no. The crease is barely visible when using apps or scrolling around the home screen, and I can hardly feel it when swiping across the display. The iPhone Duo’s unconventional shape means it can do things you wouldn’t be able to do as easily with a regular phone. Prop it open like a tent or stand it up like a book while the screen is locked, and the display will turn into a bedside clock, digital photo frame or calendar. Certain apps like the camera and Apple Fitness Plus will shift to the top portion of the screen when folded halfway like a laptop – but that depends on whether developers program their apps to do it. When the phone is open, you can take selfies with the phone’s rear cameras while viewing a preview on the cover screen, which came in handy when I was shooting the video for this review. The iPhone Duo can run two apps on screen at the same time, which was useful for situations that involved looking up information or viewing content in multiple apps. You can, for example, drag and drop an image straight from the Photos app into a text message when both apps are on screen. I also used split screen mode to show a friend my Halloween costume and the movie character it’s based on at the same time. While this is convenient, it’s probably not the reason you’re going to buy an iPhone Duo. The Duo’s inner screen is best used when dedicating the whole thing to a single app like Netflix. And the display has a matte finish, which reduces glare and doesn’t smudge easily. But many apps, including popular ones like Google Maps, Gmail, Call of Duty Mobile, and Uber weren’t updated to take full advantage of this big screen when I tested the Duo before launch. Some apps looked like floating windows in the middle of the tablet-sized screen. These apps can expand to occupy more of the display, but they still don’t fill the whole space. Other apps were updated to occupy most of the display but still had a black bar along the side. That’s what you see when developers haven’t updated their apps using Apple’s latest software development tools, as the company lays out on its website. The good news is that more apps have been updated even during the few days I’ve had the phone, including Google, TikTok, Instagram and Threads. But the uncertainty of not knowing how an app is going to look feels inconsistent and can be jarring – which is an area where Android has had a head start. The apps that are optimized for the Duo provide a glimpse of what’s possible. My favorite app so far is the puzzle platform game Planet of Lana, which looks gorgeous and colorful on the Duo’s larger screen. I also really liked using Apple Books, which lets you view pages on either side of the screen when the display is slightly folded like a real book. (Amazon’s Kindle app is one of the many apps that hasn’t been updated yet). Apple’s Messages and Mail apps also show your inbox on the left and messages on the right so that you can see everything at once. But how is it as a regular phone? For its price, the iPhone Duo should be able to do everything a regular phone can do and more. My biggest concern was that the design would make it feel awkward to use when closed, but typing and swiping on the cover screen feels surprisingly natural and comfortable. I’ve even come to prefer the Duo’s wider keyboard over the one on my iPhone 18 Pro. Still, there was a learning curve at first. I kept accidentally hitting the Siri button, which is located on the Duo’s side, when I meant to press the volume keys on the top of the phone. I also didn’t realize that you must have an app open before you can use split screen mode, rather than just opening a new app and dragging it to one side of the display from the home screen. Battery life is reasonable and in line with what you’d expect from a new phone. My battery was usually down to 35% or 46% by the time I went to bed, although that will always vary depending on which apps you’re using and how often you’re using the tablet screen compared to the cover display. The iPhone Duo has cameras that are similar to the iPhone 18 Pro’s but with one key difference: there’s no telephoto camera. That means zoomed-in photos won’t look as crisp or clear compared to ones taken on the iPhone 18 Pro, although shots captured on both phones looked similar otherwise. The biggest question I get about the iPhone Duo is whether it’s worth the $2,000. That’s tough to answer considering it costs more than a month’s rent for most Americans . The only reason you should even consider it is if you really want a screen that’s bigger than you’d find on any other phone but still fits in your pocket. My advice? Wait until developers have had more time to optimize their apps before you decide. While the Duo is compelling, apps still have catching up to do.

cnn.com.title: North Korea tells border troops to take ‘resolute action’ if South threatens their safety
cnn.com.text: North Korea has told its border troops to take “prompt ​and resolute action” if South Korean forces threaten their safety, state media ​said on Wednesday, raising the risk of a clash along the ⁠heavily armed frontier. The report came a day after Seoul pledged to punish “resolutely” any ​further provocation by Pyongyang if North Korea acted on threats to strengthen its military ​posture along the border. North Korean Army Marshal Pak Jong Chon inspected fortifications on the border with South Korea on Tuesday, accompanied by Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong ​Un, KCNA reported. Kim Yo Jong said new firepower units had “taken their firing positions” at ​the border, KCNA reported. Tensions between North and South Korea have risen since Pyongyang began fortifying its ‌border ⁠in April 2024. The two countries are separated by the Demilitarized Zone that was established when the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953. Seoul says Pyongyang has sent up to 7,000 workers to the border this year, with about 50 ​crossings of the ​Military Demarcation Line, ⁠which bisects the DMZ, to South Korea’s side of the border. On Wednesday, North Korea rejected Seoul’s allegations, with Pak dismissing ​the claim as an “absurd assertion” designed to shift blame, KCNA reported. The ​North Korean ⁠army knew where the border lay “better than any others” and was only doing what it should within its own territory, Pak said, urging soldiers to turn the border ⁠into an “impregnable ​fortress.” South Korea said North Korean mines caused ​a border blast last month that seriously wounded two of its soldiers, and called on Pyongyang to suspend the ​fortification work.

cnn.com.title: Fact check: Contrary to Trump’s claim, no law required Roger Marshall to sue his patients
cnn.com.text: No law required Sen. Roger Marshall to file lawsuits against patients who had unpaid medical bills. Marshall, a Republican obstetrician-gynecologist who is in a competitive race for re-election in Kansas, has faced criticism over a New York Times report that he launched hundreds of lawsuits against patients who had outstanding bills and charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate. The Times reported that dozens of Marshall’s patients were arrested after missing court dates in collections cases. President Donald Trump has claimed that Marshall was required by law to take aggressive action to collect from patients – though Marshall has also said that he wrote off many patients’ bills. Trump has even asserted that Marshall could have been arrested if he didn’t do what he did. “He was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request, strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people. And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said at a Kansas rally on Monday, invoking an antisemitic trope. “And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law, he would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability.” But state and federal laws give doctors and hospitals wide latitude to choose to forgive patients’ debts over financial hardships or to pursue unpaid bills using methods gentler than litigation. Marshall himself claimed to CNN’s Manu Raju last week that “each year, our hospital gave away millions of dollars of charity care” and that “we wrote off hundreds of people’s bills every month.” Similarly, there is no law that would subject a doctor to potential arrest for choosing to forgive the bills of patients who had difficulty paying. And there is no law requiring 18 percent interest on unpaid bills. The Kansas City Star, which has also debunked Trump’s claim, found that the 18 percent rate was unusually high in the state even among the Kansas medical practices that chose to sue patients. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to repeated CNN requests to identify the law that supposedly mandated his actions. The White House, in an unsigned email, mentioned two connected federal laws, one criminal and one civil, that require healthcare providers who serve patients enrolled in federal benefit programs to make a reasonable effort to collect payments from most patients – but the White House didn’t mention that those laws allow providers to forgive the money owed by people who can’t afford to pay. In fact, one of the very articles the White House sent as supposed evidence explicitly says that the federal inspector general overseeing health services “has confirmed that it will not enforce the (two laws) against providers who waive copays or deductibles due to genuine financial hardship.” We’ll discuss that further in the next section of this article. “I’m not aware of any federal or Kansas law that requires doctors to collect money owed by patients and holds them criminally liable if they do not,” Christopher Garmon, an associate professor of health administration at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, said in an email. “Doctors, and other health care providers, are given broad discretion to decide how to bill patients (e.g. how much to set as billed charges) and how much to collect in certain situations. It is common for health care providers to provide charity care to low-income uninsured patients and to write off unpaid bills as ‘bad debt.’” Garmon noted that “there are requirements that health care providers must make good faith efforts to collect patient cost-sharing to participate in certain health plans or programs (e.g., Medicare).” But he added, “I’ve never heard of a doctor going to jail for failure to collect money owed by patients.” Barak Richman, a professor and co-director of the health law program at The George Washington University, said in an email: “Unless Kansas is remarkably different from the states that I’ve studied, I can say with confidence that the decision to sue a patient on an unpaid debt is up to the provider’s discretion, and it’s an action that most providers decide not to take.” Federal anti-kickback law allows doctors to forgive debts Trump suggested in his Monday speech that the law he is referring to “has to do with the collection of money for the federal government.” Marshall told Raju last week that “when and if it happened – like every other hospital, nonprofits alike and other doctors’ offices – some of those people by law have to go to collections. There has to be some effort to go to collections. Or otherwise, CMS (the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services), Medicaid, we’d be in violation of that as well.” The White House’s unsigned email mentioned a criminal law called the Anti-Kickback Statute, under which doctors can face prison time, and a civil law called the Civil Monetary Penalties Law, under which doctors who violate the anti-kickback law or other statutes can face additional penalties. But the website of the federal health department’s inspector general makes clear that no legislation requires doctors or hospitals to sue patients. In undated guidance to physicians, the website says, “Where the Medicare and Medicaid programs require patients to pay copays for services, you are generally required to collect that money from your patients. Routinely waiving these copays could implicate the (Anti-Kickback Statute) and you may not advertise that you will forgive copayments.” But here’s the key: The advice immediately continues by saying, “However, you are free to waive a copayment if you make an individual determination that the patient cannot afford to pay or if your reasonable collection efforts fail. It is also legal to provide free or discounted services to uninsured people.” Separately, the inspector general’s office explained in 2022 that to meet the “reasonable” standard, a healthcare provider’s collection effort must include issuing a bill and then taking actions “such as subsequent billings, collection letters, telephone calls, or personal contacts with the responsible party.” Lawsuits are not on the list of required actions. In addition, the office said that in cases where a healthcare provider has determined that a patient is “indigent,” they don’t have to make the usual reasonable collection efforts. Marshall is running against Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a pastor. Hamilton campaign spokesperson Tyson Brody said in an email, “Roger Marshall chose to sue his patients. He chose to charge them 18% interest, and he and his personal lawyers chose to file warrants for their arrest. These were not normal business practices – they were extreme and predatory.”

cnn.com.title: Sky burials, sealed mouths and an ancient stone carving: The Turkish archaeological site filled with Stone Age secrets
cnn.com.text: You never know what might be hiding at the bottom of your garden. On a good day in New York, it may be a rusty safe crammed full of gold and diamonds. On a not so great one in Australia, it could be 102 venomous snakes. And on an unassuming morning in 2020 among the foothills of Turkey’s eastern Taurus Mountains, it was a prehistoric human settlement brimming with millennia-old mysteries. For the villagers of Sayburç, it turned out the strange T-shaped stones that had been so useful in the construction of their garden walls were, in fact, pillars resembling abstract humans, structures synonymous with the pre-agricultural hunter-gatherer people that carved them roughly 11,000 years prior. After the pillars were identified by staff from the nearby Şanlıurfa Museum, excavation began in earnest the following year and new discoveries have emerged at a relentless pace ever since, shedding new light on a Neolithic age that marked the dawn of a settled human lifestyle. As of 2026, roughly 70 Neolithic structures have been unearthed in Sayburç, a tightly packed mixture of dwellings and communal buildings where ancient humans lived, died and — based on the presence of stone basins and grinding equipment — processed grain and potentially made beer in one of the earliest-known villages. Yet arguably no finding has captured imaginations quite like one of the first to be unearthed at the site: five figures carved on a stone bench within one of the settlement’s five communal buildings. From left to right, a bull is depicted from the side, its huge horns — chiseled as if looking from above — pointing toward the onlooking form of a slightly squatted male figure. His six- fingered left hand is raised, while his right grips some kind of object. It is the other man on his right, however, that stands out. The only figure carved in high relief, bulging eyes and thick lips face toward the room, seemingly unbothered by the two giant leopards — tails curled and jagged teeth visible — inches away on either side. Taken together, it represented the earliest known carved stone depiction of a narrative “scene,” Istanbul University archaeologist and site excavation lead Eylem Özdoğan explained in a 2022 research paper, published in the academic journal Antiquity. While other Neolithic sites around Şanlıurfa province, known collectively as Taş Tepeler (Stone Hills), feature similar architectural techniques and iconography, none have examples of the horizontal format of a progressive, linked story. “If you look at the region, especially Göbeklitepe and Karahantepe, you will see all these figures as individual depictions,” Özdoğan told CNN’s Erica Hill. “But here you see them in relation. They are pieces of a story.” Plot holes What the actual plot of that story is though, remains a mystery. That’s not to say there has been a shortage of theories: Özdoğan has gathered as many as she can from professionals and amateurs alike in recent years. Some have interpreted the scene as simply a dramatic retelling of encounters between man and beast, pointing to the prominence of the bull’s horns and the attacking stances of the leopard pair. Others have taken that reading further as depicting a rite of passage, of individuals facing down mighty animals as a form of initiation or coming-of-age test. Concepts of fertility and continuity have also been inferred. The male figure between the leopards grips an emphasized erect penis in his right hand, leading some modern scholars to read a pre-farming tale of survival and virility. Phallic imagery is found across Taş Tepeler; Karahan Tepe’s so-called Pillar Room depicts 10 upright pillars carved in phallic form. As the leading authority on Sayburç, Özdoğan doesn’t cling to one hypothesis. While she welcomes the various readings, she ultimately has little interest in theorizing the exact narrative. “Everybody has different stories, different imaginations, about what they see on the reliefs,” she explained. “I think all of them are right and have some kind of truth in it, but it is not possible to know the exact story they were representing.” “It is important for me as an archaeologist how those stories worked for them … To know the real story is not really important for me. Maybe it is because I will never know it.” For Özdoğan, the implications of how important the reliefs were for the community that carved them are ample cause for intrigue. They represent the collective memory and values of a people finding its feet during the transition to a more sedentary life, the archaeologist explained, displayed publicly for all to see. With little distinction between public and private life, Özdoğan sees the reliefs as the “glue” that helped bind these early societies together. “I believe that they had many rules about life and daily activities. Everything was decided — nobody could just do whatever they liked,” she said. “To follow all these conditions, they needed a kind of strong discourse. I think the relief is describing such a perspective about daily life and beliefs.” Bones and belts A host of other discoveries have followed at Sayburç, with the Neolithic remains comprehensively complete despite some damage incurred during later Roman settlement and the establishment of a modern village in the mid-20th century. The relationship of the site’s earliest settlers to death has been an ongoing source of fascination. The dead were often buried within inhabited dwellings, excavations revealed, sometimes beneath the floor in careful arrangements, suggesting that the deceased endured as parts of the household. Last year, a small carved figure apparently depicting a deceased person with their mouth seemingly sealed, stitched or closed shut, was uncovered. In some places, animal bones were mixed with human bones. Combined with the repeated imagery of scavenging birds across Taş Tepeler — most notably a pillar at Göbekli Tepe depicting a vulture beside a headless human body — it has led some to theorize whether the burials point to an intentional process of excarnation, whereby scavengers were offered the dead’s flesh as part of a wider “sky burial” funeral practice. Pillars have similarly served as a rich vein of intrigue, not least the T-shaped structures dotted around — and even within — Sayburç’s Neolithic dwellings. Often featuring carved arms and belts, the stones have been interpreted as anthropomorphic structures that were possibly treated as human-like. One pillar in a distinct building at the center of the village features a carved human face at its bedrock base. With the pillar directly opposite a large niche set into the wall and neighbored by other pillars featuring carvings of a leopard and a pig, Özdoğan sees the room arrangement as deliberate, even if the exact story remains elusive. “We can see that the public art is more visible than the other regions … this shows us that they want to show their tradition in a visible way,” she said. “They are oral cultures, so they cannot pass the norms and the traditions by writing. They pass all these traditions by words and stories. This probably helped them to remember the stories, what they need to know, and transmit it to new generations.” To help ensure those stories continue to be told, Özdoğan is currently involved in a plan to turn the Sayburç site into an open-air museum. “This will help save the settlement for the future,” Özdoğan said. “It’s a really unique thing to see.”

cnn.com.title: How to catch a glimpse of the dazzling Orionid meteor shower
cnn.com.text: The Orionid meteor shower creates one of the most brilliant displays in the night sky each fall — but this year’s celestial event may have a dimmer showing due to a bright moon. Unlike the recent Draconid meteor shower, a treat for early sleepers, the Orionids will reward those who stay up late or rise in the dark hours before dawn. The shower, which appears every year as Earth passes through the debris trail left by Halley’s comet, is predicted to peak at 2 p.m. ET Wednesday. That means the best time to spot the quickly flashing meteors will be during the overnight hours between Wednesday and Thursday, according to EarthSky. Sky-gazers across the Northern and Southern hemispheres should start to see meteors zip by after midnight local time. Just a few days before the full moon rises on October 26, the waxing gibbous moon will be 76% illuminated Wednesday night, according to the American Meteor Society — which could make it harder to spot the shower during parts of the viewing period. But the bright moon is expected to set a few hours before sunrise, so sky watchers will have an optimal window to spot up to 20 meteors per hour. The Orionids bring streaking fireballs Orionid meteors are known to fly by at high speeds, streaking through Earth’s atmosphere at 41 miles per second (66 kilometers per second). Some of the glowing space rocks can leave behind lingering trains that remain visible for seconds to minutes, while larger debris fragments can create exceptionally luminous fireballs as they break up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. The Orionids appear to originate from the direction of the Orion constellation, hence the shower’s name, but meteors will be visible across the night sky. Halley’s comet completes one orbit around the sun about every 76 years, shedding dust and debris along the way. Earth crosses paths with this trail every October — and again each May, which results in the Eta Aquariid meteor shower. But unlike our planet, Halley’s comet moves in a retrograde orbit — meaning it moves in the opposite direction around the sun. For the best view of the Orionids, avoid areas with intense light pollution, such as urban areas with streetlights. Sit in a reclining lawn chair or lie on your back to get a wide view of the sky. Upcoming meteor showers There are more meteor showers to look forward to as the end of the year approaches. Here are the peak dates to glimpse these dazzling celestial events, according to the American Meteor Society.

bbc.com.title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

bbc.com.title: Celebrity shark guided out of South Korea canal refuses to swim out to sea
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A famed dusky shark in South Korea is continuing to linger near a canal that it was ejected from on Wednesday.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after it was spotted swimming in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
For weeks, rescuers tried in vain to get her back to the open sea, using nets to guide it out.
On Thursday, authorities said they had reinforced barriers to prevent Bukangi from returning. But it has yet to swim out into the open sea, and instead has been seen circling back repeatedly to the mouth of the waterway.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans gathered at the park overlooking the canal, cheering and waving goodbye to the shark.
But then, on Thursday morning, Bukangi reportedly swam back into the canal after breaking through a barrier installed by authorities.
For some time, Bukangi was trapped in a tight space between two layers of nets in the canal.
Rescuers freed it by removing the outer layer, and have since fortified the remaining layer of nets to prevent it from going back in.
Since then, authorities said, Bukangi has been swimming further out but keeps circling back.
A government official told the BBC on Thursday afternoon that rescuers have concluded their operations to free the shark.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi has already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors.
Its popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as it appeared to be injured and was not eating.
Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout.
There were concerns that it would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
Before this week's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

bbc.com.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
bbc.com.text:
- Published
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.
It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.
OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
What is the flaw?
Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.
Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.
It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.
What websites have been affected?
The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.
That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.
Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.
