(Hernandez and the police department did not respond to emailed questions. Reached by phone, the department’s deputy chief did not answer questions about the response.)
The two firefighters, listening to their radios, hustled to the upstream bridge, prepared rope and watched the water. Minutes later, a call came on the radio: two children were trapped in a house at the upstream RV park. Swiftwater technicians at the park waded in and saved them.
During the crucial minutes immediately after the Trotters’ children were swept downstream, no one had clear information. According to multiple firefighters, the department briefly thought it had found all the missing children. Experts told ProPublica that such chaos and misinformation is common during disaster response. But the experts also said it can be mitigated by having good dispatch systems and adequate staffing.
Records show that Ruidoso firefighters fielded 34 emergency calls on July 8 once flooding started, and the department has stated it made more than 60 rescues.
Despite the deaths, first responders say the village’s leadership has not learned needed lessons and has continued to prioritize tourism at the expense of public safety.
By this summer the village had finally installed its voice-activated sirens and reversed its position on the standard ones: The village would now use them during floods.
Hall had planned for all firefighters to be trained as swiftwater technicians. But in February, the firefighters, many of whom worked second jobs to make ends meet, unionized. The department’s plans changed, with Hall sending firefighters to get a lower-level certification that limited their ability to perform rescues in rushing water.
In April, senior Ruidoso Fire Department officers held a meeting during which they discussed Hall’s leadership. ProPublica reviewed a recording of the gathering. An officer said Hall, who did not attend the meeting, still wouldn’t pre-position extra firefighters. “How many people are going to die?” the officer wondered aloud during the meeting.
Hall declined to respond to questions about the meeting and the allegation that he hadn’t pre-positioned enough firefighters to avoid paying overtime.
Once monsoons arrived this year, multiple rescuers say, Hall rarely stationed off-duty firefighters in vulnerable areas. Sometimes in the afternoons, when it was most likely to rain, multiple firefighters weren’t in town. To promote tourism, Ruidoso had signed a contract with Contour Airlines to provide flights between Denver and the village. During takeoffs and landings emergency medical workers had to be present at the airport, 17 miles from where Trotter and Stark were rescued.

theintercept.com.title: Google DeepMind Engineer Resigns in Protest of Pentagon Contract
theintercept.com.text:
Sofia Liguori, a research engineer working at DeepMind, resigned in protest this week from Google’s pioneering artificial intelligence laboratory. Unlike a wave of other AI researchers who have quit over fears AI might someday turn against humanity, Liguori stepped down over concern about her employer’s current practices.
Disenchanted and disturbed by Google’s military contracts with the U.S. and Israel, Liguori says she could no longer stand working at a company that was going to help kill people or help build technology that “automatically makes it easier to escalate the brutality of war.”
Liguori joined DeepMind in 2023 and began working on AI systems aimed at more efficiently routing power through the electrical grid, a peacetime engineering problem. But as she learned of Google’s Project Nimbus contract, which furnishes Israel’s military and top weapons manufacturers with a suite of advanced artificial intelligence tools, she began to question her role in the company, and the company’s role in the world. The day after Google announced its classified military AI contract with the Pentagon in April, Liguori staged a personal sick-out, using a combination of sick leave and holiday time off to cease her work.
In a letter she sent internally informing DeepMind and her colleagues of her resignation, Liguori urged them to “stay human” in the face of military work. “I no longer believe that our technology will have a net positive impact on society. I think there’s a fantasy world where AI can help decarbonize grids, cut waste, protect ecosystems, and benefit humanity,” she wrote. “But it’s not this world, and it’s not this type of general purpose AI we are racing to develop. Racing to deploy agentic AI in this society and historical moment is a terrible idea, and will definitely be a net evil.”
The Intercept spoke to Liguori, an Italian national living in London, where DeepMind is headquartered, about how she came to view her employer as dangerously powerful. During a series of interviews by phone and via text, which have been edited and condensed for length and clarity, she explained her moral opposition to military work, the role of unionization in dissent, and what hope engineers and scientists might have for influencing their companies.
What was it about DeepMind that made you want to work there?
I had a high opinion of DeepMind; it was a dream company. It had this aura of being a research-oriented place where you could sit close not just to computer scientists, but real scientists and researchers and people with backgrounds in biology, in physics, in mathematics, in ecology, in anthropology.
You joined in 2023, by which point the company had already been involved in Project Nimbus. Were you aware of that project at the time?
Not really. The first year when I joined, I was very new and very isolated in my team. Google DeepMind is a huge company and if you’re not in the right channels, you end up being very siloed. I didn’t know about Project Nimbus, but when the Gaza war escalated, I discovered it. I immediately looked for some internal resistance movement to join, but I didn’t find anything.
I discovered [Google employee advocacy group] No Tech for Apartheid, but I thought it was mainly a U.S. organization. I didn’t know how to connect with colleagues that share concerns, so the only thing that I did was buy a Palestine hoodie and go to the office with that.
In the summer of 2024, I went on maternity leave because my daughter was born, and during maternity leave I was watching news from Gaza every day. I was really suffering experiencing maternity and watching a livestreamed genocide, and every time I was thinking of my company’s complicity in that. I thought about not coming back to work at all.
When I was due to come back, I met a colleague that had basically taken my role in my team before maternity leave, and they were actually leaving for ethical reasons. They put me in contact with the union movement and No Tech for Apartheid. And so I found other colleagues fighting against this.
How and when did you learn of the company’s contracts with the U.S. military?
By the time they started engaging with the U.S. Department of War, [Editor’s note: July 2025] I was already involved in activism. By this winter we saw the GenAI.mil contract materializing, and for me, this was a very clear indication of the company’s intentions. At the same time Google ramped up the security level authorization for Cloud: IL6, which is the level required to handle classified workloads.
The combination of the two — signing this non-classified deal with the Department of War, and ramping up security level — really meant that we wanted to use AI for war, on the battlefield. Even if the internal narrative was, “No, don’t worry, it’s just for administrative purposes, just to process documents.”
What was happening internally?
Internally there was a lot of conversation in specific channels where people were complaining, but leadership never really answered anything. I had some of my posts deleted.
What had you written, and did you ever get any sort of answer as to why this stuff was deleted?
I had several posts deleted because they contained the word “genocide,” and I was told that genocide is an intrinsically violent word, and so I was violating internal policies. Even when my posts weren’t deleted, I often had conversations with my manager and HR telling me that my tone was not appropriate because I was too aggressive and that I should raise my concerns in different ways.
They basically wanted us to send [internal HR] tickets to raise our concerns. The problem is that when you do that, you receive semi-automated answers with absolutely no content, nobody is engaged on the concern you have raised. There’s no discussion at all, you don’t even interact with a human. It’s a lot of administrative and bureaucratic steps you have to follow to raise concerns. What I wanted was discussion and what I wanted was very clear answers from leadership.
They tell you this is not the place to raise concerns, try to go through this other channel. This is the common technique. They always tell you to do something else, try to make you tired, and you will never get an answer.
[Editor’s note: The Intercept asked Google about Liguori’s criticism of both the contract and how discussion is handled internally. Spokesperson Tom Hewett responded: “We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles. We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns – ranging from business ethics to misconduct – and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind.”]
I think the reason why you would be opposed to Project Nimbus is pretty straightforward: genocide. What were your specific concerns about or opposition to the Department of War contract?
I’m against the use of AI for targeting and in warfare in general, not only for autonomous weapons. I’m against AI for war, and I don’t think a commercial company like Google should have anything to do with that.
AI for targeting is very dangerous; it creates a system where it’s easier to escalate the brutality of war. The first problem is the opacity introduced in the definition of targets and the dehumanization that follows. In principle, if you have to define targets, if you want to define Hamas combatants, you have to think what it actually means and come up with a definition.
But with these systems, you can bypass the definition. The system itself comes out with a definition. You don’t even question it, you just blindly rely on the definition as the ultimate truth. The person just becomes a set of aggregated data points. All individuality is lost, all humanity is lost in in this process.
It becomes a system that dehumanizes people. It becomes a rubber stamp because the human brain cannot process all this information. You keep a person that formally approves it, but they don’t, they cannot, meaningfully evaluate the output. This links to the accountability gap: Everyone in the kill chain can plausibly say that they didn’t decide.
What did you do to protest the Department of War contract internally?
Mainly messaging on corporate channels to inform colleagues, and speaking with them in person. I tried to channel the widespread dissatisfaction and indignation over the contract into the collective movement we are building, into our union effort. [Editor’s note: DeepMind employees voted to unionize in May.] Many people still don’t know there are other colleagues organizing against these contracts and for a more ethical Google DeepMind.
When you are alone and you lose faith in your company, and you stop believing your work makes a positive difference, you can only become disillusioned and frustrated, and you ultimately end in acceptance and cynicism, or you leave. Finding you are not alone, and joining a collective movement, gives a much better option. It gave me the strength to stay, at least for a year.
I also co-organized a demonstration in February in front of the office. The scope was broader than just the Department of War, but the December GenAI.mil launch had given me a deep sense of urgency, and that’s why I organized the demonstration. I knew something like the classified deal was coming, and I knew this meant legitimizing Nimbus-style collaborations to become the standard. The demonstration was for Gaza and for any use of AI in war. We had banners with “No AI in the kill chain” and “No Gemini for Genocide.”
Has your work as a research engineer contributed to your concerns about this technology being used to kill? How has your technical knowledge informed your opposition?
Understanding how these systems work makes it easier to see where the problem is. Understanding statistical aggregation, and how easy it is to just delegate responsibility, delegate decision-making, makes a difference. But I think it’s more important to do some philosophical reasoning here.
Do you have concerns about the reliability of the technology?
I am concerned about unreliability. But I don’t think you should ever look at unreliability separate from a discussion of why AI in warfare is wrong by itself.
A lot of the time what I hear is a focus on error, for example, the Minab school attack. If we focus only on the error, we are basically saying that if there was no error, these systems for automated targeting are OK.
Were there people within Deep Mind who were supportive of this contract or military work generally?
Yes, it was actually a very debated topic. I think there is broad consensus on the Anthropic red lines, which are fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance.
But on whether to use AI for military purposes, this is a much more debated topic, and a lot of people buy the narrative of us-versus-them: That we need to defend ourselves against Russia, against China, and so on.
What was your thought process on deciding to leave the company over this?
It was a very challenging year. I came back as a new mom with a full-time job, a baby to handle, I had some health issues, and I was committing to activism basically on the side. Many people told me, you can slow down, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t stay in the company and just go on with business as usual. I really felt we needed to stop the Department of War contract because I perceive that contract as normalizing what happened in Gaza — the kind of tech-powered, AI-powered, brutal war that was tested in Gaza was getting approved to become the standard of war.
I don’t think petitions have a great effect in general. The [DeepMind] petition summarized my disillusionment from us not having done more during the year to prevent this from happening. For me, really, we should have gone on strike this year. We should have stopped working.
In the U.S., there is a lot of defense of these contracts on the basis that it’s important for national security. That might be persuasive if you’re American. But Americans are a pretty small minority on the planet. I’m curious what your perspective is on that kind of rationale as someone who lives in another country, who is a citizen of another country.
There’s been discussion about that as well. A lot of Europeans were actually scared of that, because the current Trump administration is not very friendly even to Europeans. What feels like national security for U.S., people feels like a threat for Europeans.
Are you aware of other colleagues at DeepMind who are going to follow what you’re doing and quit?
Some have quit already, some publicly and some silently. There have been many people leaving because of ethical reasons. Not all of them publicized it.
Do you think it’s possible for workers to change something like the Pentagon contract? What is the worker movement inside Google/DeepMind missing that would allow for that kind of change?
I think it’s possible, but it requires a real commitment and readiness to take some risk. Ultimately, I think we need a workforce ready to strike to oppose these contracts. Currently, many people are too scared to even express an opinion publicly. The company was very effective at creating a pervasive sense of fear, which induces self-censorship.
What I tried to show my colleagues this year was exactly that the boundaries we perceive and we retreat behind are not the real boundaries — that we can speak out and keep our jobs. Most of the times the reaction is intimidation in meetings, mentions of policy violations, but nothing else follows. Obviously, there are some boundaries, but they are much farther then the perceived ones.
I also took a day off and demonstrated in front of the office in February, together with University College London BDS [Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement] staff and a few other colleagues. I faced literally no consequences for that because it’s a trade union activity in my spare time, and in the U.K., we are protected for such an action. This can be a form of soft strike.
As I write in my letter, if we fail to challenge these restrictions, we internalize them and become diminished versions of ourselves. And I think that in an era of increasing surveillance and authoritarianism, that’s something to reflect on. I have felt much freer since I found the courage to speak out and take some risks. It’s empowering. Fighting this fear is a big part of our task in the union movement we are trying to create in Google DeepMind.
The next step would be a real strike. I always tell my union friends that if I see any Google workers strike, I can die happy.

This is not hyperbole.

theintercept.com.title: Trump’s Obsession With Somalia Isn’t Just Racist. It’s Been Lethal.
theintercept.com.text:
The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar.
In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent. Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar.
Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms, in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee, and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation.
“This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.”
Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.”
Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept.
With the Somali community, Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric, without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
“As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.”
Trump’s War on Somalia
Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists.
The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance.
U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants.
The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email.
“Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.”
The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher. A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “five terrorists” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.”
Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “fourth-world nation,” says that it “stinks,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.”
His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country.
A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises.
Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump.
Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people, according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government, no military, and is “not even a country.”
The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million.
“I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.”
During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “the ongoing armed conflict” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.”
Bringing the War Home
Despite the increase in violence, according to Pentagon statistics, the administration terminated Somalia’s TPS designation earlier this year. More than 1,000 Somali asylum-seekers have been ordered deported since February; more than half the deportation orders involve Somalis living in Minnesota, a nearly tenfold increase from 2025, according to a Minnesota Star Tribune investigation.
About 84,000 of the 260,000 people of Somali descent in the U.S. live in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area, according to the Census Bureau’s annual American Community Survey. The overwhelming majority are American citizens. Almost 58 percent were born in the U.S. and 87 percent of foreign-born Somalis are naturalized citizens.
The administration targeted that Somali community during a violent immigration crackdown in and around Minneapolis known as “Operation Metro Surge” during late 2025 and early 2026. “I don’t want them in our country,” Trump said in December 2025. The next month, he said: “Every one of them should be forced to leave this country, including Ilhan Omar.”
During Metro Surge, federal agents shot and killed protesters Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti. They, like Omar and hundreds of drone strike victims in Somalia, were labeled as terrorists by the administration without providing evidence.
During Trump’s second term, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have also arrested hundreds of Somali people, with reports of assault and mistreatment at the hands of federal agents.
Trump recently seemed to call for vigilante violence and threatened to back it with federal force. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this month. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Hussein, of CAIR-MN, said Trump’s rhetoric was endangering the Somali community. “Every few weeks, he’s literally going on a tirade. And I don’t think he’s ever spoken about other people the same way. He literally put out the message saying, ‘go fight them. I’ll come and help’ on social media,” he told The Intercept. “We’ve seen bullying. We’ve dealt with harassment. We’ve have some assaults.”
Trump has routinely demonized Somalis by tying the broader community to a high-profile fraud case: the alleged theft of $250 million from a pandemic-era program that provided food for children. The former leader of Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of the case, is white, although most of the defendants in the related cases are of Somali descent. “The Somalians, they’re crooked as hell,” Trump ranted at a Cabinet meeting in May, with the administration offering escalating and unverified claims, including reference to a “$19 billion Somali fraud scandal.”
The Trump administration’s effort to denaturalize and deport Omar is part of a broader push to strip naturalized Americans of their citizenship, with those of Somali descent specifically singled out. “I would do it in a heartbeat if they were dishonest,” Trump said in an Oval Office interview earlier this year. “I think that many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.”
Trump’s border czar Tom Homan said on Saturday that he had been “told they have a strong case” against Omar. “Of course, if you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody. We’ve done it before,” he told Fox News. The rarely used denaturalization statute has been most famously employed to strip citizenship from Nazi war criminals, like John Demjanjuk, a former death camp guard and retired U.S. autoworker convicted on 28,060 counts of being an accessory to murder.
Mohamed, who in 2022 became the first Somali woman elected to the Minnesota Senate, called out Trump’s push to expel Omar as a grave threat to the country. “If the president can threaten to denaturalize and deport a member of Congress, no one is safe,” she told The Intercept. “This is a test of our democracy, and even Republicans should be speaking out about it. If we don’t defend the rights of Ilhan Omar, Somali-Americans, immigrants, and Trump’s political targets, we lose everything.”

lemonde.fr/en.title: Suspects in West Bank settler attacks on US photojournalist and French mayor put under house arrest
lemonde.fr/en.text:
All but one of the suspects arrested over recent settler attacks on an American photojournalist and a visiting French mayor in the West Bank have been released from detention and placed under house arrest, their lawyers said.
Israeli police had announced on Monday, October 19 the arrests of 10 people implicated in the attacks in the occupied Palestinian territory, where violence by Israeli settlers is on the rise but perpetrators are seldom prosecuted.
Honenu, a legal aid organization that often represents Israeli soldiers and settlers, said that all but one of the suspects had been released to house arrest.
Lawyer Assaf Gonen said in a statement that their arrests had only been "for show," and were "intended to satisfy media pressure and foreign interests." The suspects have not been identified.
On Friday, photographer Heidi Levine, 65, who was on assignment for The Washington Post, was taken to hospital with broken vertebrae after being beaten by settlers while covering the West Bank's annual olive harvest.
A day later, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries who was on a goodwill visit.
The attacks drew international condemnation, but mixed messages from the Israeli government. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race in elections next week, has tried to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base and has cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent attacks.
His tone has drawn unusually strong criticism from the opposition, which has accused him of tarnishing Israel's image.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'As if I were a criminal': French high schoolers recount arrests and police custody
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Leïla was released from police custody without any charges, but was required to attend a citizenship course. "All for exercising my right to protest; it's kind of funny, really." That happened 10 days before the nationwide protests on Saturday, October 17, which were marred by violence and looting in many cities across France. When we met her in Versailles at the start of the month, the 17-year-old high schooler had just spent a night in a cell, sharing it with a 13-year-old girl suspected of pickpocketing. Now that she was "finally" given the chance to speak, Leïla seized it with adolescent passion. She had "never been one to hold her tongue."
Leïla, Nino and Inès are among the nearly 7,000 minors arrested since the start of the high school student movement at the end of September, out of approximately 8,000 in total. The three teenagers agreed to speak to Le Monde about this defining moment in their young lives. They described not only their demands but also the circumstances of their arrest, their hopes and worries, and how their relationship with institutions – especially the police – and with protest itself has changed. Each invited a parent to join the conversation, offering a nuanced perspective marked by ambivalence, as their parents wavered between fear for their child and pride in seeing them take a stand for a cause all described as "just" and "legitimate."
"But they don't always do it in the best way," said Nora, Leïla's mother. Both chose to use pseudonyms, worried that speaking out might affect the high school student's future. For the same reason, the others preferred not to give their last names. "The credibility of your action lies in the way you carry it out," Nora continued. "But come on, Mom! Even when we're peaceful, [the police] charge at us and throw tear gas at us!" her daughter protested.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Iran denounces police violence in France and urges Paris to guarantee 'freedom of protest'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Iranian authorities decried what they called France's "double standards." Since high school protests began in France at the end of September, Tehran has repeatedly criticized the use of what it considered "disproportionate force" by law enforcement and called on France to respect "freedom of protest." In January, when Iranian authorities violently suppressed a wave of demonstrations in Iran, French President Emmanuel Macron had publicly called for respect for the right to peaceful protest.
On Monday, October 19, after a weekend of unrest in Paris and other French cities, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghtchi called on the French president to heed the demands coming from the streets. "The French people demand wholesale change, including freedom of assembly. Listen to the future of France, Mr. President," he wrote without irony on the social media platform X.
In January, far from listening to the demands of Iranians, the regime crushed the movement with violence, the full toll of which remains unclear due to weeks-long internet shutdowns and pressure to silence victims' families. According to evidence gathered by human rights organizations, this crackdown – which continues with near-weekly executions – has been the bloodiest in the history of the Islamic Republic of Iran against protesters.

lemonde.fr/en.title: E-commerce giant eBay to cut 1,000 more jobs, about 9% of workforce
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US e-commerce platform eBay will cut some 1,000 jobs, or about 9% of its workforce, a spokesperson told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Wednesday, October 21, following an initial round of layoffs in February.
The company informed staff of the cuts on Tuesday, according to a statement from the spokesperson. The step was taken "to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said, adding that eBay is "committed to supporting them through this transition with care and respect."
It had 12,300 employees at the end of 2025, before announcing a first round of layoffs in February affecting 800 jobs.
When presenting first- and second-quarter results earlier this year, executives at the San Jose, California-based company made no mention of the job cuts.
Near-stagnant revenue followed by growth
After several difficult years marked by near-stagnant revenue, eBay returned to growth in 2025 and saw an acceleration in the first half of this year.
In July, the group took control of clothing resale site Depop for $1.2 billion, seeking to capitalize on the rise of the secondhand apparel market.
In early May, video game retailer GameStop made an unsolicited takeover offer valuing eBay at $55.5 billion. GameStop chief Ryan Cohen argued that the group was poorly managed and not innovative enough. The board ultimately rejected the offer, with investors questioning how the deal would be financed.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'A Man of His Time': A 'miracle' political film that resonates from the French left to the far right
lemonde.fr/en.text:
At last, some good news – something sorely lacking these days. The most riveting film we've seen in a long time, A Man of His Time (French title, Notre Salut) by Emmanuel Marre, is a hit in theaters: 215,000 admissions in its first week, nearly 500,000 after two weeks. That is a far cry from the 8 million for the latest Spider-Man, but here, audiences spend two hours and 40 minutes with an ordinary collaborator in the Vichy administration, portrayed by Swann Arlaud, who is in virtually every scene, delivering a minimalist performance centered on the banality of evil. Add to that a 15-minute opening set in a claustrophobic setting likely to put off the impatient, no action scenes, a puzzling narrative, bold formal choices, no romantic plot or dramatic effects, evil lurking in the details, largely improvised dialogue and a handheld camera.
"A Man of His Time shows that French audiences can embrace highly innovative forms," said Eric Marti of Rentrak, a box office analysis company. This is exemplary of a cinephile country, supported by a unique production industry and theater network. How high will admissions climb? Word of mouth is excellent, but for the film to surpass one million tickets sold, it will need to break out of its comfort zone. For now, it has been embraced by audiences in major cities – led by Paris, where no other film is doing better, which is remarkable – and by an affluent, highly educated public. Since its release, the number of theaters screening it has continued to grow, reaching smaller towns and rural areas. That will be the real test.
Perhaps A Man of His Time's greatest achievement is being a major political film that tackles difficult debates, yet has been acclaimed by Le Monde and Le Figaro, Libération and Le Journal du dimanche, Télérama, Causeur, Les Inrockuptibles, and the magazine Eléments. In short, it has won over the entire political spectrum, including the far right, all without provoking controversy – something of a miracle in an age when it takes very little to discredit a work.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Canadian publisher says novelist Orélien used AI to write novel
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The publisher of top-selling Haitian-Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien said Wednesday it had confirmed that he used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C'était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die).
Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer. But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations.
"New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process" of the novel, a Boréal statement said. The publisher announced it was "ending its professional relationship" with Orélien. Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI's use in the writing process "and we will likely never have a definitive answer."
It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyze the various drafts. "The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents," Boréal added.
Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence. That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien "subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information," the publisher said. The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.
'Slander and heresy'
The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the shortlist for France's top book prize, the Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100-percent probability it contained computer-generated text.
In a statement to Agence France-Presse (AFP) earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations "slander and heresy."
"Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms," he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP. "But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut."
He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Liberation he used AI "in the creative process" for "historical research."
"I've explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don't think my words count for anything," he said, adding that what he is currently experiencing has "gone way too far."
Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 "on the corner of a table" and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT.
The author fled his native Haiti following a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest. In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making "unacceptable mistakes" in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics.
"I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot," he wrote. "But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own."

lemonde.fr/en.title: War in Ukraine: Bolstered by Trump's support, Putin refuses to back down
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Steve Witkoff arrived alone in Saint Petersburg, Russia, claiming he wanted to advance peace. On Wednesday, October 21, the American businessman's solo trip to present proposals to Vladimir Putin – proposals discussed the previous day with Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo – was in itself a clear sign of a certain casualness on the part of the Trump administration. It demonstrated a refusal to engage in any show of strength between Washington and the Russian leader.
Welcomed at the Konstantin Palace, the "Russian Versailles" in Strelna on the outskirts of the former imperial capital, Witkoff spent two and a half hours in talks with the former KGB lieutenant colonel, who was accompanied by his loyal associates: financier Kirill Dmitriev and Yuri Ushakov, his special adviser for diplomatic affairs.
At the end of the discussion, Donald Trump's personal friend – who has no diplomatic experience – came away with no concessions from Russia regarding Ukraine that might have signaled the end of the war. The Russian leader, firmly in control as he faced an intimidated and dazzled Witkoff, laid out his conditions. Talks bringing together Ukraine, Russia and the United States, which Western diplomats had expected to take place in the coming days in Abu Dhabi, would now not happen before November 10, Ushakov said.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Greek youth, inspired by France, protest over living conditions and deteriorating public education
lemonde.fr/en.text:
"From Greece to France, we are fighting for public and free education," chanted demonstrators in 50 Greek cities on Wednesday, October 21. Some 20,000 turned out, according to police, to protest the decline of public education and the lack of resources allocated to young people. Protesters carried banners with slogans in French such as "Study or survive?" and "The world is ours." These references reflect Greek youths' desire to see their movement as part of a broader wave of protest across Europe, as well as a shared anxiety over the cost of studies and the decline of public services.
"The government is not investing in our universities, the infrastructure is deteriorating, and student support is practically non-existent," said Tasos Mertzianidis, a philosophy student. "Students are forced to pay exorbitant rents. Those who cannot afford it are forced to drop out."
The housing crisis has become one of the main sources of financial instability for young Greeks. According to real estate consultancy Geoaxis, rents increased by more than 115% in Athens and by over 93% in Thessaloniki over the past 10 years. In a country where the minimum wage has stood at €920 per month since April, despite successive increases since the financial crisis, housing costs remain a heavy burden.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Walmart unveils tools allowing AI agents to shop for customers
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US shopping giant Walmart on Wednesday, October 21, unveiled tools allowing artificial intelligence agents such as Meta's Muse to shop on behalf of its customers, taking the opposite approach to rival Amazon, which bars outside AI agents from its platform.
AI agents are programs that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user's behalf – such as searching for products, comparing prices and completing a purchase – rather than only answering questions as chatbots do.
Tech companies including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta are investing heavily in agents, which much of the industry sees as the next phase of the AI boom that followed the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
Anthropic rolls out Claude Duet
Anthropic on Wednesday released a preview of Claude Duet, an agent that works in the background across users' connected apps and can make online purchases with their approval.
Its archrival OpenAI launched its own always-on agents, called Dots, last month.
Muse, which Meta launched in September and has made available only in the United States and Canada, has been downloaded more than 10 million times, according to an analysis of third-party data by Sensor Tower.
Walmart said it would launch "Agent Profiles" within the next month, letting customers register each AI assistant they use as a separate profile within their Walmart account so that purchases made by the agent appear apart from their own.
Customers will be able to require approval for every purchase or let an agent buy on its own up to a spending limit they set, such as $50, $100 or $200, and delete a profile at any time.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Offices of European Parliament far-right group raided in EU funds investigation
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The second day of the European Parliament's session in Strasbourg had just begun on Wednesday, October 21, when police entered the fourth floor of the Louise-Weiss building, where the offices of the secretary general of the Patriots for Europe, a far-right parliamentary group led by France's Rassemblement National (RN), are located. Investigators searched the premises for evidence supporting suspicions of financial crimes involving Identity and Democracy (ID), the RN-led group that preceded Patriots from 2019 to 2024.
The search, carried out by France's Central Office for Combating Corruption and Financial and Tax Offenses, was revealed at midday on Wednesday by the head of the RN delegation in the European Parliament, MEP Jean-Paul Garraud, in a post on X. A source close to the investigation confirmed that the raids targeted Belgian national Philip Claeys, a former member of the far-right Vlaams Belang party who became the key administrator for the RN's parliamentary groups. Belgian police also raided his offices in Brussels, the European Parliament's other seat. When contacted, Claeys did not immediately respond. He remains secretary general of Patriots, which is chaired by RN president Jordan Bardella.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Soaring debt costs deal another blow to French economy
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On Wednesday, October 21, France briefly borrowed at rates above 5% to finance its debt on the markets. This symbolic threshold, the highest since 2002, delivered another blow to the already struggling French economy, as the increase is set to have far-reaching consequences.
In its forecasts published on October 14, the French Institute of Economics (IFE) estimated that growth could reach 0.5% in 2027, in a scenario where 10-year rates average 4.5% through the end of next year. "If rates were to remain consistently above 5%, that prediction would have to be revised downward," explained Mathieu Plane, deputy director of the analysis and forecasting department at the IFE. This scenario cannot be ruled out, given the significant uncertainty surrounding France's economic and political situation today.
The shock triggered by the violence accompanying protests in cities across France on October 17 has heightened investor concerns about France's ability to rein in its budget deficit ahead of the presidential election in April 2027. But the fallout goes further. It "could also discourage households from spending, deter tourists and prompt companies to postpone their investments," added Charlotte de Montpellier, economist at the Dutch bank ING. "The loss of confidence now represents the greatest economic risk," she said. The rise in rates "exacerbates already difficult financial conditions and is likely to weigh further on investment and economic activity." Business investment accounts for 12.2% of GDP and household investment for 4.5%.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French MEP Rima Hassan mounts political defense at trial for glorifying terrorism
lemonde.fr/en.text:
What exactly was the 10th criminal chamber of the Paris judicial court judging on Monday, October 19, and Tuesday, October 20? Was it Rima Hassan, the compulsive French-Palestinian tweeter, or Rima Hassan, the member of the European Parliament from La France Insoumise (LFI, radical left)? Was it a criminal offense of glorifying terrorism, or an elected official's freedom of expression? Was it the Tel Aviv airport attack, carried out on May 30, 1972, by a Japanese Red Army commando, or the Hamas terrorist attacks of October 7, 2023? Was it the Palestinian people's right to resist, or the need to combat antisemitism?
Too many questions for a single trial, too many contradictions for a calm hearing. On Tuesday afternoon, the prosecution sought a 10-month suspended prison sentence and two years of ineligibility from public office for Hassan, immediately drawing the ire of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI leader and candidate for the 2027 presidential election, who wrote on X: "Macron's supporters have sunk into the shame of all abuses of power and servility in the face of Netanyahu's demands." The court will deliver its verdict on November 30.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Protesters injured after French police continue using new stun grenade
lemonde.fr/en.text:
At 12:36 pm on Place de la République in Paris, during the October 17 protests, a stun grenade thrown by French riot police exploded at the legs of a journalist wearing a press patch. The video above shows its explosion and the woman lying on the ground, her jeans torn, with multiple wounds on her legs.
The grenade that injured this woman was a GL-304. It was adopted by French law enforcement in 2025 in order to "reduce as much as possible" the risk of injury. Le Monde can confirm that during a protest on Tuesday, October 13, four days before October 17, 36 GL-304 grenades were used, with at least two causing serious injuries, and two others involved in dangerous incidents.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Macron makes surprise visit to Saudi Arabia
lemonde.fr/en.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron visited Riyadh on Wednesday, October 21, for a surprise "solidarity" visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in the kingdom since Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month. The unannounced trip sent a strong signal to his oil-rich Saudi ally as Riyadh comes under near-daily attack. It was part of a Gulf tour to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France, following a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs.
Facing criticism of his Gulf tour in France, Macron told reporters he was just "doing his job" to "ease tensions" over gas prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France. "There must be no sign of febrility," he said. "I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post."
Macron met de facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Elysée Palace said. The pair agreed that Saudi Arabia would supply France with additional diesel "for as many months as necessary" and consult on expanded security cooperation and infrastructure projects to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, the palace added.
Earlier, the presidency said the visit would "demonstrate France's solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory." In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A Houthi maritime blockade is also threatening the kingdom's oil exports. Macron's visit comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to rally Western support in the face of Houthi attacks.
'Personnel deployed'
Earlier on Wednesday, Macron said France had sent troops to help shield the key Saudi oil terminal of Yanbu on the Red Sea from Houthi attacks, while insisting it was important that "discussions resume" with the group. "For the past eight days, we've had personnel and capabilities deployed (in Yanbu); we're working with Saudi Arabia in this direction, and so we have a defensive role to play," he told reporters in the Qatari capital.
The world's biggest crude exporter had relied on Yanbu to export its oil after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war.
Last month, Macron said in a televised interview that France would send "military means" to help shield the Yanbu terminal from Houthi attacks. On Tuesday, the UK government announced it would deploy British fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against increasing attacks.
During his tour, Macron secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, as well as two terawatt-hours of LNG per month from Qatar.
In July, a truce in Yemen dating back to 2022 fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized government-held territory along the Red Sea coast. In response, the Saudi air force has frequently targeted the group in support of pro-government forces.

welt.de.title: Trump erwägt Einsatz von „Mutter aller Bomben“ gegen iranische Berganlage
welt.de.text: Die USA und Israel haben einem Bericht der „ New York Times (verlinkt auf https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html) “ zufolge konkrete Pläne für neue Militärschläge gegen den Iran nach den amerikanischen Zwischenwahlen am 3. November ausgearbeitet. Vorgesehen sei eine kurze, intensive Operation gegen mögliche Ziele wie die Energieinfrastruktur, Atomanlagen sowie Raketen- und Drohnenbestände. Ob US-Präsident Donald Trump die Angriffe genehmigt, ist offen. Die Zeitung beruft sich auf amerikanische Regierungsvertreter und weitere Personen, die über die Beratungen informiert seien. US-Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth habe bei einem Besuch in Israel in dieser Woche mit Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu über neue Angriffe gesprochen. Beide Streitkräfte hätten zudem ihre Übungen verstärkt und über dem Irak Angriffsmanöver trainiert. Einige amerikanische Planer setzen dem Bericht zufolge darauf, mit einer intensiven dreitägigen Angriffswelle so großen wirtschaftlichen Schaden anzurichten, dass Teheran diplomatische Zugeständnisse macht. Die Verhandlungen laufen parallel zu den militärischen Vorbereitungen weiter. Streitpunkte sind insbesondere das iranische Atomprogramm und die Kontrolle über die Straße von Hormus. Zweifel an Wirkung der „Mutter aller Bomben“ Zu den möglichen Zielen gehört laut „New York Times“ die tief unter einem Berg gelegene Anlage Kuh-e Kolang, auch „Pickaxe Mountain“ genannt, die mit dem iranischen Atomprogramm in Verbindung gebracht wird. Trump erklärte in der vergangenen Woche in einem Interview mit Newsmax, einen Einsatz der Bombe GBU-43/B gegen die Anlage zu erwägen. Die als MOAB bekannte Waffe trägt den Spitznamen „Mutter aller Bomben“. Die von der Zeitung befragten Waffenspezialisten bezweifeln jedoch, dass sie die unter Granitgestein geschützte Anlage zerstören könnte. Die MOAB ist zwar die sprengkraftstärkste konventionelle Fliegerbombe im Arsenal des US-Militärs, aber keine tiefeindringende, bunkerbrechende Waffe wie etwa die GBU-57 A/B Massive Ordnance Penetrator,  die bislang gegen die Atomanlagen bei Fordo und Natans eingesetzt worden sein sollen (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/newsticker/dpa_nt/afxline/topthemen/article256286494/im-fokus-von-israel-und-den-usa-die-iranischen-atomanlagen.html) . Die MOAB explodiert oberhalb des Bodens und entfaltet eine großflächige Druckwirkung, statt tief in den Untergrund einzudringen. Militärvertreter warnten zudem, dass das für den Abwurf benötigte langsame Transportflugzeug durch die iranische Flugabwehr gefährdet wäre. Dass der Einsatz der Bombe beschlossen wurde, geht aus dem Bericht nicht hervor. Auch die Zielauswahl ist offenbar nicht abgeschlossen: Während Energieanlagen grundsätzlich als mögliche Ziele genannt werden, wollen einige Verantwortliche Raffinerien und Ölinfrastruktur aussparen, um weitere Preissteigerungen zu vermeiden. „Pickaxe Mountain“ befindet sich in der Provinz Isfahan, ganz in der Nähe der Atomanlage Natans. Trump soll Angriff bereits kurzfristig gestoppt haben Bereits Anfang dieses Monats standen die USA und Israel laut dem Bericht kurz vor erneuten Angriffen. Beide Streitkräfte hätten umfangreiche Vorbereitungen getroffen und ihre Luftstreitkräfte in höchste Alarmbereitschaft versetzt. Trump habe die Operation jedoch kurz vor Beginn verschoben. Auch zuvor habe er in diesem Jahr mehrfach eine Rückkehr zu größeren Kampfhandlungen abgelehnt. Die vollständige Zusammenziehung der vorgesehenen amerikanischen Kräfte werde erst Anfang November abgeschlossen sein. Dazu zählten drei Flugzeugträger, Tausende Marineinfanteristen, Kampfflugzeuge und Spezialkräfte. Ein Vertreter des Weißen Hauses erklärte der Zeitung, die Regierung kommentiere keine Militärpläne, „die möglicherweise existieren oder auch nicht“. Trump halte alle Optionen offen, um eine iranische Atomwaffe zu verhindern. Iran droht mit ausgeweiteten Gegenangriffen Iranische Vertreter kündigten dem Bericht zufolge in sozialen Medien an, bei neuen Angriffen weitere Ziele ins Visier zu nehmen. Neben Handelsschiffen und Energieanlagen könnten auch Rechenzentren und Untersee-Internetkabel betroffen sein. Die Vorstellung, eine weitere Angriffswelle werde nach 72 Stunden beendet sein, bezeichnete ein hochrangiger Berater der iranischen Verhandlungsführung als „Fantasie“. Zweifel an der amerikanisch-israelischen Strategie äußerte auch die frühere Pentagon-Verantwortliche für Nahostpolitik, Dana Stroul. Die bisherigen Angriffe, Sanktionen und die amerikanische Seeblockade hätten die iranische Führung nicht zu substanziellen Verhandlungen bewegt. Weder Trump noch Netanjahu hätten überzeugend erklärt, warum weitere Kriegshandlungen daran etwas ändern würden.

welt.de.title: Marine Le Pen baut Vorsprung in Umfragen nach Unruhen in Frankreich aus
welt.de.text: Frankreichs rechtsnationale Politikerin Marine Le Pen hat in der ersten Wahlumfrage zur Präsidentschaft seit den  Ausschreitungen vom Wochenende (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/plus6ad5c846843996518cba5823/frankreich-wie-der-staat-die-kontrolle-verlor-wir-standen-im-blindflug.html)  weiter zugelegt. In der neuen Ifop-Umfrage mit Blick auf die Wahl im kommenden Frühjahr erreicht Le Pen je nach Kandidatenkonstellation 34 bis 38 Prozent der Stimmen im ersten Wahlgang, wie die im Auftrag der Sender LCI und Sud Radio sowie der Zeitung „Le Figaro“ erstellte Befragung ergab. Im Vergleich zur vorherigen Ifop-Umfrage gewann sie in vergleichbaren Szenarien ein bis zwei Prozentpunkte. Eine noch vor den Ausschreitungen vorgelegte Odoxa-Umfrage sah die Spitzenpolitikerin des Rassemblement National (RN) ebenfalls je nach Konstellation bei 38 Prozent, weit vor allen anderen Kandidaten. Le Pen fordert Durchgreifen gegen Randalierer Le Pen hatte nach den Unruhen bei Sozialprotesten am Wochenende ein härteres Durchgreifen der Behörden gefordert und von einer tiefgreifenden Vertrauens- und Autoritätskrise gesprochen. Für die Ausschreitungen machte sie die Regierung von Präsident Emmanuel Macron und die Einwanderungspolitik verantwortlich. Ob die Unruhen den Zuwachs in der Umfrage verursacht haben, lässt sich aus den Daten nicht ableiten, auch weil keine Fragen in Bezug auf die Ausschreitungen gestellt wurden. Die Ifop-Umfrage sieht den Anführer von Frankreichs Linkspartei, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, in der ersten Wahlrunde auf Platz zwei mit 15 bis 20 Prozent. Dicht dahinter rangieren ähnlich stark der Bewerber der Sozialisten, Raphaël Glucksmann, sowie der Mitte-Politiker Édouard Philippe. Amtsinhaber Macron kann nach zwei Amtszeiten nicht mehr antreten. Wer tritt gegen Le Pen an? Für die zweite Wahlrunde sieht die jüngste Ifop-Umfrage Le Pen unabhängig vom Herausforderer in sämtlichen Szenarien vorn. Wie die Chancen stehen, dass die Tochter von Parteigründer Jean-Marie Le Pen im kommenden Frühjahr tatsächlich zur Präsidentin gewählt wird, hängt entscheidend auch davon ab, wer für die anderen politischen Lager ins Rennen geht. Diese aber haben sich, bis auf die Linkspartei und die Sozialisten, noch nicht klar sortiert. Allerdings könnte Le Pen ihre im Juli bereits von einem Berufungsgericht bestätigte  Verurteilung wegen Veruntreuung von EU-Geldern (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6a4ce983bb0cf80de56a0e78/marine-le-pen-in-berufungsprozess-verurteilt-praesidentschaftskandidatur-aber-moeglich.html)  einholen, gegen die sie Revision eingelegt hat. Je nachdem, wie schnell das Kassationsgericht darüber entscheidet, könnte der 58-Jährigen mitten im Wahlkampf das Tragen einer Fußfessel drohen.

welt.de.title: „Sind so nah dran wie noch nie“, sagt Trump über Friedensabkommen – Russland bombardiert Kiew
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump hat sich zuversichtlich über ein baldiges Ende des Ukraine-Kriegs geäußert. „Vielleicht sind wir jetzt so nah dran wie noch nie“, sagte er am Mittwoch (Ortszeit) in Washington. Jedenfalls sei eine Einigung seiner Einschätzung nach nähergerückt: „Wenn man kurz vor einer Einigung steht und sehr heikle Verhandlungen führt, verhängt man keine Sanktionen.“ Trump verteidigte seine Entscheidung, ein weitreichendes neues Sanktionspaket gegen Russland vorerst nicht umzusetzen. Die nach dem im Juli gestorbenen US-Senator Lindsey Graham benannte Gesetzesvorlage sieht verschärfte Sanktionen vor. Graham hatte sich für das Paket eingesetzt. Kritik an Trumps Entscheidung komme von „Leuten, die nicht wissen, wie das Leben funktioniert“, sagte der Präsident. Der Verzicht auf die Sanktionen habe dazu beigetragen, die Freilassung des US-Amerikaners Stephen Hubbard zu ermöglichen, argumentierte Trump. Hubbard war am Mittwoch freigekommen, nachdem er mehr als vier Jahre in Russland inhaftiert gewesen war. Russland warf ihm vor, als Söldner in der Ukraine gekämpft zu haben. Die Anwälte Hubbards bestreiten das. „Wenn man diese Sanktionen verhängt hätte oder wie auch immer man sie nennen will, hätte man ihn vergessen können“, sagte Trump über Hubbard. „Man hätte ihn nie wiedergesehen. Er wäre für 25 Jahre wieder im Gefängnis gewesen.“ Trump äußerte sich nach einem Treffen  seines Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff mit dem russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6ad882a8438656aeb2fad5f7/ukraine-krieg-russland-zu-neuen-gespraechen-mit-usa-und-ukraine-bereit-witkoff-nennt-putin-menschenfreund.html) . Witkoff hatte die Diskussionen als „konstruktiv“ bezeichnet. Es gebe aber „noch wichtige Arbeit zu erledigen“, sagte er weiter. Witkoff hatte sich am Mittwoch in St. Petersburg mit Putin getroffen, nachdem er tags zuvor in Oslo mit dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj zusammengekommen war. Nach eigenen Angaben überbrachte er Putin „Ideen“ und „einige Dokumente“ für ein Ende des inzwischen fast fünf Jahre andauernden Kriegs. Der Kreml zeigte sich anschließend zur Wiederaufnahme der Verhandlungen mit Washington und Kiew bereit. Die von Witkoff übermittelten Vorschläge der Europäer und der Ukraine für eine Friedenslösung bewertete der Kreml aber kritisch. Russland bombardiert Kiew Kiew ist erneut Ziel heftiger russischer Angriffe geworden. Wie Bürgermeister Vitali Klitschko am frühen Donnerstagmorgen im Onlinedienst X mitteilte, schlugen die ganze Nacht über Raketen in der ukrainischen Hauptstadt ein. Die Bewohner mussten demnach in Schutzräume ausweichen, sechs Menschen wurden verletzt. Die ukrainische Luftwaffe warnte in den frühen Morgenstunden vor „weiteren ballistischen Raketen in Richtung Kiew“ und forderte die Bewohner auf, in Schutzräumen zu bleiben. Bei einem Angriff wurden laut Klitschko Teile einer U-Bahn-Brücke beschädigt. Betroffen sei die Südbrücke über den Fluss Dnipro, teilte ⁠er auf Telegram mit. Auch aus Moskau wurden Angriffe gemeldet. Der Bürgermeister der russischen Hauptstadt, Sergej Sobjanin, teilte mit, dass in der Nacht 630 Drohnen in Richtung der Region gestartet worden seien. Die meisten von ihnen seien von der russischen Luftabwehr zerstört worden. Zwei Menschen seien verletzt worden. 163 der Drohnen steuerten laut Sobjanin auf Moskau zu.

welt.de.title: „Wow. Der hat voll einen abbekommen“ – Trump lobt Prügel für Wahlkampf-Störer
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump ist bei einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung in Pendleton im US-Bundesstaat South Carolina mehrfach von Protesten unterbrochen worden. In der ersten halben Stunde seiner Rede störten etwa zehn Demonstranten die Veranstaltung. Bei einem der letzten Proteste kam es zu einer Rangelei im Zuschauerbereich. Trump reagierte mit den Worten „Wow“ und „Das hat mir gefallen. Ich habe das beobachtet“. „Der hat voll einen abbekommen“, sagte Trump, nachdem einer der Störer in der Menschenmenge zu Boden ging. „Das war großartig“, jubelte Trump. Danach fragte er anerkennend: „Wer ist der Typ, der diesen Schlag gelandet hat?“ Als Sicherheitskräfte den Protestierenden aus dem Saal brachten, sagte Trump, der Mann, der zugeschlagen habe, habe ihn an den früheren Boxweltmeister Evander Holyfield erinnert, der Trump zu der Veranstaltung begleitet hatte. Trump warb in South Carolina für die Kandidatin Darline Graham, die für die Republikaner in den Senat einziehen soll. In knapp zwei Wochen finden in den USA die Zwischenwahlen statt, bei denen die Republikaner ihre dünne Mehrheit im Kongress verteidigen wollen. Bei derselben Veranstaltung überraschte Trump mit der Idee weiterer Umbenennungen von Gewässern. Er erinnerte daran, dass er bereits per Erlass den Ontariosee in „Lake America“ und den Golf von Mexiko in „Golf von Amerika“ umbenannt habe. Nun sei ein Fluss an der Reihe, so Trump. Dabei habe er unter anderem den Hudson River und den Mississippi in Betracht gezogen. Derzeit denke er jedoch am meisten darüber nach, einen der beiden Ozeane – Atlantik oder Pazifik – umzubenennen. „Ich werde weder Trump noch Amerika auf einen anderen Ozean schreiben“, fügte Trump hinzu. Das dürfte viele erleichtern.

welt.de.title: „Schaurige Warnung an alle Amerikaner“ – Frankreich wird für die Republikaner zur Wahlkampfwaffe
welt.de.text: US‑Präsident Trump nutzt die Bilder der Randalierer in Paris, um die Stimmung kurz vor den Midterms zu drehen. Er und seine Mitstreiter setzen dabei auf eine zentrale Botschaft.

welt.de.title: Atempause für Putin – „Es hätte eine Chance gegeben, Russland zur Waffenruhe zu bewegen“
welt.de.text: Kaum ein Staatschef versteht so viel vom Krieg wie er: Tschechiens Präsident Petr Pavel war einst Generalstabschef seiner Armee und schließlich der mächtigste General der Nato. Jetzt lenkt er die Tschechische Republik durch die Russland-Krise – und ist tief besorgt. Am Donnerstag verkündete Russlands Machthaber Wladimir Putin, dass er zu erneuten  Verhandlungen mit den USA und der Ukraine (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6ad882a8438656aeb2fad5f7/ukraine-krieg-russland-zu-neuen-gespraechen-mit-usa-und-ukraine-bereit-witkoff-nennt-putin-menschenfreund.html)  bereit sei. Pavel warnte vor direkten Gesprächen zwischen den USA und Russland, ohne Europa einzubeziehen. Es sei nicht möglich, über europäische Sicherheit zu verhandeln, während die Europäer außen vor blieben. Deshalb müsse Europa zunächst eine klar formulierte, eigene Verhandlungsposition entwickeln. Den russischen Herrscher hält Pavel für „falsch informiert und paranoid“. Seine wichtigsten Aussagen: Europa muss einen Verhandlungsführer finden Europa benötige zunächst „eine interne Debatte über eine umfassendere europäische Position“, sagte Pavel. Im Anschluss solle eine Person oder eine Gruppe von Führungspersönlichkeiten bestimmt werden, die Europa bei Verhandlungen vertritt – nicht unbedingt Vertreter der EU oder der Nato, sondern Politiker mit einem klaren Mandat der anderen. Warum weder Amerika noch Russland Europa derzeit ernst nehmen, erklärt Pavel so: „Sie sehen, wie gespalten wir sind, wie schwach wir sind, wie lange es bei uns dauert, bis wir überhaupt eine Entscheidung treffen.“ Ändere sich das nicht „sehr schnell“, drohe Europa, irrelevant zu werden. Ein „Bonbon“ für Putin Ein Angebot an Putin könnte nach Pavels Vorstellung so aussehen: „Wenn wir einen Prozess in Gang setzen, der zu einem Ende des Konflikts in der Ukraine führen würde, dann gäbe es keinen Grund, weitere hybride Angriffe zu starten, insbesondere wenn am Ende ein Bonbon wartet. Und wenn ich von einem Bonbon spreche, meine ich die Wiederaufnahme von Wirtschaftsbeziehungen, Zusammenarbeit und Handel, was für Russland ziemlich verlockend ist.“ Eine Lockerung der Sanktionen sei allerdings nur denkbar, wenn Russland wieder zu einem respektierten Partner werde – also Waffenstillstand und Friedensverhandlungen zustimme. Zugleich sieht Pavel Anzeichen für Kriegsmüdigkeit beim Gegner: Russlands Ressourcen seien erschöpft, der Konflikt dauere inzwischen länger als der Zweite Weltkrieg. „Die soziale Lage dort ist wirklich nicht gut, die wirtschaftliche Lage ist sehr düster.“ Moskaus falsche Behauptungen Putins Behauptung, die Nato plane einen Angriff auf Russland, wies Pavel entschieden zurück. Er habe trotz höchster Sicherheitsfreigabe der Nato nie einen Plan gesehen, der auf eine Offensive auf russischem Territorium abgezielt hätte: „Alle Nato-Pläne sind defensiv.“ Russland verliere zudem jeden Monat Zehntausende Soldaten – allein im September waren es rund 50.000 Getötete und Verwundete. Das übersteige bei Weitem das Tempo, in dem Moskau seine Verluste durch Rekrutierung ausgleichen könne. Als eigentliches Ziel des Kremls nannte Pavel, das Leben in der Ukraine unerträglich zu machen und möglicherweise eine neue Flüchtlingswelle nach Europa auszulösen. So solle demonstriert werden, dass die Ukraine nicht gewinnen kann. Über Putins Geisteszustand sagte Pavel, der Kreml-Chef vertraue kaum jemandem und habe obsessive Angst davor, getötet zu werden. Sein kleiner Kreis von Vertrauten filterte die Informationen, die Putin erreichten. Die Folge: Putin sei vermutlich überzeugt, die Militäroperation verlaufe erfolgreich. „Ich glaube, dass er in mehrfacher Hinsicht falsch informiert wird.“ Eskalation zwischen Europa und Russland Ohne Änderung der Lage werde der Krieg „auf unbestimmte Zeit weitergehen, weil keine der beiden Seiten gewinnt“, warnte Pavel. Er verglich ihn mit einem modernen Ersten Weltkrieg: eine Todeszone, in der es praktisch keine Bewegung gebe. Europa habe dabei schwere Fehler gemacht. Einige Länder hätten gezögert – erst bei gepanzerten Fahrzeugen, dann bei weitreichender Munition, dann bei Raketen, dann bei Flugzeugen. Das habe die Ukraine nicht nur Territorium gekostet, „sondern vor allem Tausende und Abertausende Menschenleben“. Pavel warnte, bei unverändertem Kurs könnte es zu einer Eskalation zwischen Europa und Russland kommen, „die schließlich zu einem offenen militärischen Konflikt führen würde“. Derzeit führe Russland einen hybriden Krieg mit dem Ziel, Zwietracht in EU und Nato zu säen und Europa von der Unterstützung der Ukraine abzubringen. Der Präsident sprach auch von einer verpassten Chance auf eine Waffenruhe. „Ich glaube, wir waren dieser Situation ziemlich nahe“, so Pavel. Das „abgestimmte Vorgehen“ von USA und Europa gegen Russlands Wirtschaft habe „positive Ergebnisse“ gezeigt, „Russland stand unter Druck“. Der Präsident weiter: „Ich denke, wenn wir das gleiche Tempo hätten beibehalten können, dann hätte es eine Chance gegeben, Russland zu einer Waffenruhe zu bewegen. Jetzt hat Russland wieder eine Atempause bekommen“ – durch Geld aus den Vereinigten Staaten für Öl, durch Hinweise darauf, dass es eine Bereitschaft zu einer Einigung ohne Europa, ohne die Ukraine geben könnte. Jetzt werde es viel schwieriger, weil Russland diese Gelegenheit nutzt, um sich dem Druck zu entziehen. „Das ist für Russland eine Art moralischer Auftrieb.“ Das Axel Springer Global Reporters Network ist eine markenübergreifende Initiative, die Scoops, investigative Recherchen, Interviews, Meinungsstücke und Analysen globaler Relevanz veröffentlicht.
